articles.title: North Korea fires intermediate-range missile, claiming evasive flight and AI features
articles.body:
Japan’s military said the missile landed in waters outside its exclusive economic zone, while South Korea's military, which often accuses the North of exaggerating its capabilities, said it travelled more than 700 kilometres.
North Korea announced Saturday that it had test-fired an intermediate-range ballistic missile, claiming the weapon can manoeuvre in flight to evade missile defences in South Korea and Japan.
The launch comes as tensions between the two Koreas run high over landmine explosions along their border.
Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said her brother oversaw the test. She called the missile "strategic", a term that suggests it is meant to carry nuclear warheads. She also claimed it can alter its trajectory at low altitudes and has unspecified artificial intelligence capabilities, which she said would make it extremely hard to intercept.
Japan’s military said the missile landed in waters outside its exclusive economic zone, while the South Korean military, which often accuses North Korea of exaggerating its military capabilities, said the missile travelled more than 700 kilometres.
North Korea claims new missile capabilities
According to South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff, the North Korean missile was fired early Saturday from the eastern coastal Wonsan area. Japan's Defense Ministry later put the distance at roughly 680 kilometres.
In her statement, Kim Yo Jong pointed to the gap between the two US allies' figures as proof that they could not follow the missile in flight.
"Whenever we applied the wavelike trajectory mode to missiles, the enemy failed to track the targets from their first skip points," she said. "There is no way to avoid this attack."
The launch followed a day after she mocked Seoul's demand that Pyongyang apologise for the 21 September landmine explosions. The blasts went off about 10 metres south of the military demarcation line and wounded three South Korean soldiers.
A joint inspection by South Korea and the US-led United Nations Command concluded that North Korea had planted the mines, and the command later found that Pyongyang had breached the armistice that halted the 1950-53 Korean War.
Seoul has also asked the North to stop fortifying the border with mines and anti-tank barriers. That work has sped up since Kim Jong Un dropped the goal of reconciliation in 2024 and branded Seoul a permanent adversary.
Kim Yo Jong, who may be the second most powerful person in Pyongyang, called Seoul's demands "utterly pathetic" on Friday and rejected any North Korean responsibility for the blasts, warning of retaliation if the South fires on troops working along the border.
Pyongyang's weapons tests are piling up
The Wonsan launch is the newest in a string of recent military displays, which also include missile tests, live-fire drills and the commissioning of a new warship. Kim Jong Un is showing off his expanding nuclear programme even as Washington urges a return to diplomacy.
Wonsan also hosted the Sept. 20 test of what state media described as a hypersonic missile system. It belongs to a family of weapons built to overwhelm missile defences in South Korea and Japan, including solid-fuel intermediate-range missiles first revealed in 2024.
South Korea's military said it had raised its surveillance level for further launches and was sharing information closely with Washington and Tokyo. The US Pacific Command said the launch "does not pose an immediate threat to American personnel or territory or to our allies."
Kim has mostly turned his back on diplomacy with the US and South Korea since his nuclear talks with President Donald Trump broke down in 2019. He has shifted his focus to Moscow, sending thousands of troops and large shipments of weapons to back Vladimir Putin's war in Ukraine. After years of heavier testing, his arsenal of nuclear-capable missiles now includes long-range systems that could potentially reach the U.S. mainland and shorter-range ones that threaten South Korea and Japan.
In August, Trump scaled back a large joint exercise with South Korea, apparently hoping to restart talks.
North Korea has brushed off the overture, insisting that Washington first end its "hostile policy", a phrase Pyongyang uses to describe US-led sanctions and joint military drills with South Korea.

articles.title: Germany’s Merz visits Kyiv amid fears of ‘hardest’ winter in war
articles.body:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz speaks to the press after meeting soldiers of the 1 German-Netherlands Corps on October 1, 2026 in Münster. | Hesham Elsherif/Getty Images
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Kyiv for a surprise one-day visit to showcase Berlin's support for Ukraine amid Russian attacks on the Ukrainian capital that continued after the chancellor's arrival.
Merz, who is in Kyiv to deliver new military, financial and economic support pledges to Ukraine, is planning to meet President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to discuss support against Russia's escalating war, particularly in the sector of air defense and long-range offensive weapons, as well as peace initiatives.
A German official said that Berlin will provide Ukraine with a new military support package worth about €1 billion, which includes missiles and drones, as well as satellite technology to help striking military targets in Russia.
Advertisement
Germany will furthermore provide Ukraine with financial assistance for the mass-production of new drones to intercept Russia's particularly dangerous high-speed jet drones. Berlin will also provide generators, substations, and repair kits worth €350 million to make the Ukrainian grid more resilient against Russian attacks.
Ukraine is facing harsh Russian drone and missile attacks on its infrastructure, power and heating plants as well as other civilian targets, which are feared to further intensify this winter.
In contrast to previous visits from Western leaders, during which Moscow had largely refrained from attacks on the Ukrainian capital, air raid sirens could be heard in Kyiv during Merz's visit. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported that Russia had struck the roadway of the North Bridge in the city. On Saturday, Russia's foreign ministry issued a warning against foreign visitors and diplomats and urged them to leave Kyiv.
This is Merz's first bilateral visit to Kyiv and his second trip as chancellor, after travelling there in May 2025 visit alongside leaders from France, the U.K. and Poland.
“If we fail to stop Moscow, sooner or later the Russian war machine will turn against us", Merz said upon arrival in the Ukrainian capital, adding: “I will tell President Zelenskyy today, 'You can continue to count on our help.'”
During a speech in Münster, Germany, Merz warned that, “in a few weeks, the fifth winter of the war will begin”, which “likely be the hardest one yet.”
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz shakes hands with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on the sidelines of the 36th NATO Heads of State and Government Summit in Ankara, on July 7, 2026. | Pool photo by Michael Kappeler/AFP via Getty Images
Ukrainians “are bracing themselves for intense ballistic missile attacks, for destroyed power plants and schools, and for damaged apartment buildings and churches. Ukraine must survive this winter, and I am convinced that it will. It can count on our help,” Merz added, highlighting German help such as new interception systems against jet drones or repairs for bombed power plants.
Merz and Zelenskyy held a call on Wednesday, which focused on convincing European and international allies like Japan to deliver more Patriot air defense missiles to Ukraine as well as procuring fresh ammunition for Kyiv's F-16 fighter jets, which are efficient in downing Russian jet drones with their onboard cannon.
Last month, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius announced that Germany would transfer Patriot PAC-2 interceptor missiles from its own stocks to Ukraine, and called on other states to follow suit.
Following the attempted drone attack on a Ukrainian cargo plane in Leipzig in August, for which Germany blamed Russia, Berlin announced that its intelligence services would help Ukraine with supplying targeting data for long-distance strikes against Russia's military as well as its industrial base.
Advertisement
Merz has refused to supply Germany's prized Taurus cruise missiles to Ukraine, despite calling for it when he was opposition leader. Yet his government delivered financial and technical assistance for the development of Ukraine's own long-range weapons. On Thursday, Zelenskyy announced the successful test of Ukraine's FP-7 ballistic tactical missile.
German Economy Minister Katherina Reiche, from Merz's center-right CDU party, joined the trip alongside representatives from a dozen German energy, chemical and drone manufacturing companies, which will participate in a German-Ukrainian economic forum in Kyiv on Sunday.
There are tensions between Merz and Zelenskyy when it comes to Ukraine's desire to swiftly join the European Union.
The German Chancellor has voiced skepticism that an EU accession would be possible in the coming years and instead proposed an “associated membership” that would grant Ukraine access to the EU's single market and an observer status in the Council of the EU, the European Commission and the European Parliament, but without any voting rights.
Merz's visit comes amid renewed attempts to seek a peace agreement between Russia and Ukraine. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, who met with his Russia counterpart Sergei Lavrov in New York last weekend, has welcomed a U.S. invite for Vladimir Putin to the G20 leaders' summit in Miami in December, saying it could be a chance for serious negotiations.
However, so far “Russia’s leadership shows no real interest in putting an end to its deeply inhumane fantasies of subjugation and conquest,” Wadephul said on Friday. “It intends to continue the war against Ukraine.”

articles.title: Germany's Merz visits Kyiv to pledge more support to Zelensky
articles.body:
US wants to hold trilateral Ukraine talks with Russia by end of October, Zelensky says
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Sunday that the US wants to broker a new round of talks with Ukraine and Russia on ending the war and hold it by the end of October. Earlier, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the city's Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River was again hit in a Russian attack during a visit by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. Read our liveblog to see how the day's events unfolded.
This liveblog is no longer being updated, thank you for following us.
Click on the link below for a recap of the day's events and stay with us for more coverage of the war in Ukraine.
Dozens detained at Communist Party rally in Moscow
Police in Moscow detained about 60 people at a rally held by Russia’s Kremlin-friendly Communist Party, the party has said.
The party said in a statement that the detentions happened as the rally was ending, and that its Moscow branch was working to get those who were detained – mostly young people – released.
The rally marked the anniversary of the Kremlin’s 1993 crushing of a parliamentary uprising.
The Telegram news channel Ostorozhno Novosti said protesters chanted slogans including “Freedom for political prisoners,” “For fair elections,” and “Down with the Tsar.”
The rally came as public frustration has been simmering in Russia during the intensifying Ukrainian drone attacks deep inside the country.
Ukrainian drones deliver new batch of food to Russian-occupied town
Ukraine's military has again used drones to deliver food and medicines to the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has said.
Oleshky, a frontline town on the Dnipro River, which separates Russian and Ukrainian forces, has been under Russian occupation since 2022.
"For months, Russia has been trying to isolate Ukrainians in Oleshky from the outside world, even obstructing the delivery of food to people facing severe shortages," Sybiha said on X.
Drones carrying food packages fly over a location given as Oleshky, in Kherson Oblast, in footage released by Ukrainian military officials. Credit: Reuters
Ukraine used heavy-lift drones to deliver food and medicines to Oleshky at the end of September.
Sybiha said that the latest delivery consisted of nearly 400 packages containing almost 4 metric tons of food and medicine.
Ukraine believes Russia shared jet-drone technology with North Korea
Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky says he believes Russia has shared jet-drone technology with its longstanding ally North Korea,
In recent weeks, Russia has sharply increased its use of jet-drones against Ukraine, which so far has no effective means of countering them other than using combat aircraft.
Asked if Russia had shared with North Korea the technology behind its latest generation of jet-powered drones, Zelensky told journalists: "Yes, of course".
"They (Russia) are sharing with North Korea all the technologies. I don't know about the ballistic and etc, but I think, yes, because North Korea helped them with missiles," he added.
Earlier in the war, North Korea supplied Russia with millions of artillery shells, and it has since provided ballistic missiles that Moscow regularly uses to attack Ukrainian cities.
India pushing for bigger role in Russia-Ukraine talks
India is seeking a greater role in brokering an end to the Russia-Ukraine war, Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar has said at a Munich Security Conference in New Delhi.
"We have been advocating (dialogue and diplomacy) for many years, and in recent months we have got a little bit more involved beyond advocacy, so we have conversations with both Russia and Ukraine in this regard," Jaishankar said.
Subrahmanyam Jaishankar (left) visited Kyiv on September 3. Credit: Efrem Lukatsky, AP
The minister, who made his first solo trip to Ukraine in September, said India was "trying to be helpful, starting with the Black Sea safety of shipping".
But he said India was also "going beyond that", including discussion on grain and energy exports and "on non-attack possibilities".
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin have close ties, and the pair met in New Delhi in September.
Germany's Merz announces new aid for Ukraine in Kyiv
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has announced a new aid package for Ukraine worth more than 1.3 billion euros ($1.5 billion) during a visit to Kyiv.
About 1 billion euros ($1.1 billion) of the package is military aid, including long-range strike weapons, combat drones and satellite technology, “so that Ukraine can also target Russian launch pads,” Merz said at a news conference.
Germany is also providing some 350 million euros ($395 million) in energy aid ahead of winter for generators, substations and repair work, he said.
Ukraine and Germany discuss LNG supply during Merz visit
Ukrainian and German energy ministers have discussed supplying liquefied natural gas through German infrastructure to Ukraine, Reuters has quoted Ukraine's energy ministry as saying.
Ukraine had previously expressed interest in increasing LNG imports and had also offered European companies the option of storing their gas in Ukrainian underground storage facilities.
Zelensky says US wants to hold trilateral talks with Russia by end of October
The United States wants to broker a new round of talks with Ukraine and Russia on ending the four-and-a-half-year war and hold it by the end of October, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
"The American side is currently in contact with Ukraine and Russia and is proposing to somehow hold a meeting at the technical level in a trilateral format by the end of October," Zelensky told reporters.
Germany's Merz unveils new military and energy aid for Ukraine
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced military aid for Ukraine worth around €1 billion ($1.13 billion) and an energy support package during a visit to Kyiv, as the Ukrainian capital came under renewed attack from Russian drones.
Merz, who was accompanied by a senior minister and several company executives, said his visit "demonstrates that we will not be intimidated. Nor will we be intimidated by a drone attack occurring at the very time of our visit."
Zelensky meets with Germany's Merz at Kyiv Russian drone strike site
Russia to intensify strikes on Ukraine after Zelensky remarks, defence ministry says
Russia said it would ramp up its pummelling of Ukraine after President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that Kyiv would increase its attacks on Russian oil refineries.
"Following Zelensky's statement ... strikes by the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation on military and military-industrial facilities, as well as related infrastructure in Kyiv and other regions of Ukraine, will be intensified," Russia's defence ministry said in a statement.
Russian strikes hit Kyiv Northern bridge as Germany's Merz visits
Moscow has once again bombed one of Kyiv’s bridges, despite the presence of German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in the Ukrainian capital. The visit was unplanned, but Merz says it was intended to show Germany’s support for Ukraine.
FRANCE 24's correspondent Gulliver Cragg, reporting from Kyiv, says traffic has resumed on the bridge, though slowly. Video shows a large hole in the roadway. Experts say the bridges are extremely solid and difficult to destroy, even with ballistic missiles.
Three injured after drone debris triggers fire at Krasnodar industrial site, authorities say
A fire broke out at an industrial site in Russia's Krasnodar region after falling drone debris struck the site in the Temryuk district, regional authorities said.
Three people were injured and were receiving medical treatment, while emergency services were working at the scene.
Germany's Merz in Kyiv as Russia steps up attacks on Ukrainian cities
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Ukraine's capital Kyiv on Sunday on an unannounced visit in a show of support for the country in its war with Russia. Merz's visit comes just a day after Russia warned foreigners and diplomats to leave the Ukrainian capital, saying that "massive" new air strikes would hit the city.
FRANCE 24's correspondent in Kyiv Gulliver Cragg has more.
Latvian PM on track to lead pro-Ukraine coalition after election win
Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs was set to retain power and form a pro-Ukrainian coalition after his centrist United List secured the biggest parliamentary election victory since Latvia regained independence in 1991.
With 97 percent of ballots counted after Saturday's election in the NATO and European Union country bordering Russia, United List was on 35.3 percent, enough for 42 seats in the 100-seat parliament.
Kulbergs, 47, came to power in May after the previous coalition crumbled over its handling of incidents in which stray Ukrainian military drones flew undetected into Latvia.
Russia strikes hit Kyiv soon after Merz's arrival
A bridge in Kyiv was hit in a Russian attack, the city's mayor Vitali Klitschko said, soon after the arrival of German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
"Impact on the road surface of the Northern Bridge. Emergency services are heading to the scene," the mayor wrote on Telegram. Air raid sirens had earlier blared, warning of drones approaching the city.
Germany's Merz in Kyiv to hold talks with Zelensky
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Chancellor Friedrich Merz would hold talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Writing on X, Sybiha said the agenda would focus on "strengthening Ukraine, our defense and resilience, and our shared European security”.
Germany's Merz arrives in Kyiv as Russia steps up attacks on Ukrainian cities
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Kyiv in a show of support as Russia intensifies its attacks on Ukrainian cities.
The aerial war has intensified, with Moscow menacing cities across Ukraine with hard-to-intercept ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones, while Kyiv has been striking Russia’s oil industry and businesses
“Ukraine is facing decisive weeks. That is why I traveled to Kyiv today with the message: You can rely on us,” Merz wrote on X, noting that Germany’s own security “also depends on the outcome of this war".
(FRANCE 24 with AP, AFP and Reuters)

articles.title: Latvian Defense Minister: Russia's hybrid attacks, not nuclear rhetoric, main concern
articles.body:
Latvia’s defense minister has played down any immediate danger after Russia’s latest nuclear warning to NATO over Kaliningrad.
“I don’t see an imminent threat at this point,” Raivis Melnis told RFE/RL in an interview in Washington on September 30, echoing NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, who said he did not take the Russian warning "that seriously".
Russia warned NATO this week that it was prepared to use its entire arsenal, including nuclear weapons, if the Western alliance attempted to cut off Kaliningrad, its heavily militarised Baltic exclave wedged between NATO members Poland and Lithuania.
In a diplomatic memo circulated to NATO member states, Moscow said it had information that the alliance was preparing an “air and naval blockade” of the territory.
The warning prompted Rutte to call on Russia to “stop the nuclear threats”, saying NATO is a defensive alliance and that “this is absolutely not called for and not helpful”. He added that Russian President Vladimir Putin knows that he cannot win in a direct confrontation with NATO.
Melnis said Russia had repeatedly resorted to nuclear threats since launching its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, arguing that Moscow uses such rhetoric to frighten Western populations, weaken support for Kyiv, and test the cohesion of the NATO alliance.
“Russia will use any means to threaten us, to bring fear to our people, to support Ukraine, and also to break our unity, cohesion, to support and just test where are those limits,” he said.
Escalation risks?
The Russian warning has nevertheless raised concern among arms-control and security specialists, particularly because of Kaliningrad’s strategic position and Russia’s evolving nuclear doctrine.
Daryl Kimball, executive director of the Arms Control Association, a nonpartisan Washington based nonprofit, told RFE/RL that the Russian threat should be taken seriously and condemned as unacceptable. He said Moscow’s language reflected what he described as a careless approach to the dangers of nuclear weapons use.
Kimball noted that NATO does not appear to be preparing military action to isolate Kaliningrad. Even if such a confrontation were contemplated, he said, using nuclear weapons in a conflict involving another nuclear-armed state or alliance could trigger retaliation, escalation, and potentially catastrophic consequences.
He argued that Moscow should instead address its concerns with NATO through diplomatic channels, saying that “rather than threatening nuclear attack, the Kremlin should reach out to NATO capitals to clarify whatever concerns Russia might have and to address those concerns diplomatically and responsibly.”
Lynn Rusten, a senior fellow at the Centre for European Policy Analysis and a former senior White House National Security Council official responsible for arms control and nonproliferation, told RFE/RL that Russia’s latest nuclear rhetoric appeared “unhinged and hyperbolic” from a Western perspective.
But Rusten also warned of a dangerous combination of factors: Russian threats and provocative hybrid warfare, NATO and Russian forces operating in close proximity, continued Western support for Ukraine, and a lack of meaningful dialogue.
She said those conditions could increase the risk of dangerous miscalculation, particularly as Russia and NATO assert competing red lines while channels for managing tensions remain limited.
“The lack of meaningful dialogue and the growing divide in security perceptions carries a grave risk of further and potentially unintended escalation and expansion of this conflict,” Rusten said.
Sylvia Mishra, nuclear policy director at the Institute for Security and Technology, said nuclear brinkmanship was not new for Moscow but should nonetheless be treated seriously.
Kaliningrad, she noted, is home to the headquarters of Russia’s Baltic Fleet and is strategically important but geographically vulnerable, surrounded by NATO members Poland and Lithuania and separated from mainland Russia.
Mishra said reported NATO air operations around the exclave in mid-August, which included aircraft with capabilities to disrupt communications, radar, and navigation systems, could have heightened Moscow’s sense of vulnerability.
She also pointed to Russia’s 2024 revised nuclear doctrine, which formally lowered the threshold described by Moscow for potential nuclear use.
Mishra said the latest warning appeared to be the first instance of Russia issuing a written diplomatic note explicitly warning that it was prepared to use nuclear weapons if the Western alliance attempted to isolate Kaliningrad.
Hybrid attacks
For Melnis, however, the more immediate threat is neither nuclear nor a large-scale Russian conventional military assault on NATO, but an expanding campaign of hybrid activity – hostile actions short of open warfare, including cyberattacks, sabotage, and the weaponisation of migration.
He said Latvia and its allies are continuously reassessing the threat, monitoring Russia’s military capabilities, losses in Ukraine, force generation, and activities such as suspected attacks on military-industrial facilities and critical infrastructure.
“We are monitoring and we are working closely with Ukrainian partners or with our NATO partners,” Melnis said, adding that Latvia’s threat assessment is a continuous process and that hybrid activity is increasing.
Melnis said he did not believe Russia currently had the capacity to launch a conventional offensive against a NATO country while sustaining its war in Ukraine.
“Russia stopped in Ukraine, they are not achieving the goals,” he said, pointing to Ukrainian counteroffensive operations and arguing that Moscow would face major difficulties trying to conduct two large-scale military operations simultaneously.
He described cyberattacks, pressure through migration from Belarus – which Minsk has been accused of facilitating to destabilise its neighbours – and other hostile activities as part of the new security environment confronting Latvia and its allies.
Latvia is also strengthening defences against drones. Melnis said the country had deployed interceptor systems and additional radar along its borders with Russia and Belarus, drawing heavily on lessons from Ukraine. NATO fighter aircraft provide another layer, while Latvia is procuring medium- and short-range air defence systems.
Melnis said Russian drone incursions could become a growing feature of the Baltic security environment, citing recent incidents involving Lithuania, Poland, and Romania. Latvia, he said, is preparing for more such incidents.
US role in European defence
Melnis was in Washington to deepen defence cooperation with the US, including discussions involving the Michigan National Guard, procurement programmes, and capability development.
He said he remains confident that the US will maintain a military presence in Europe despite adjustments to deployments in individual countries. US forces, he said, remain in Latvia, and Washington continues to recognise the strategic importance of the region.
At the same time, Melnis said European allies must assume a greater share of the burden for their own defence. He credited US President Donald Trump with pushing NATO members to increase defence spending, saying Latvia is committed by law to spending at least 5 percent of gross domestic product annually on security beginning next year.
NATO members agreed at their 2025 summit in The Hague to spend 5 percent of GDP annually on defence and defence-related priorities by 2035, up from the alliance’s previous 2-percent benchmark. Latvia has moved faster, with its parliament requiring national defence spending of at least 5 percent of projected GDP from 2027.
But Melnis said greater European responsibility would go hand in hand with continued US support.
“The United States will provide. They will be there. They will fight with us if needed,” Melnis said, while stressing that Europe must do more.
This story was originally published by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL), partners of LRT English.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Kyiv to increase oil refinery attacks because of Moscow’s winter strategy, Zelenskyy says
articles.body:
- Ukraine will increase its attacks on Russian oil refineries, but won’t target civilians, because of a new policy of airstrikes by Moscow designed to force people to abandon Kyiv and other cities, Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said. Ukraine’s intelligence service has obtained documents showing the Russian ruler, Vladimir Putin, has issued a new doctrine of military attacks on a much broader range of civilian targets ahead of winter, Ukraine’s president told Reuters. “We saw documents and we know that they allow them to attack infrastructure, logistics, and especially to attack in the cities, in the villages, everywhere, roads, schools, hospitals,” he said. “To pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities: this is the goal of the operation.”
- “We have to respond in any way [we can]. With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refiners: what gives money to them for this war,” Zelenskyy said. “But we will not respond, of course … on any civilian objects.” Russian attacks on Saturday in Ukraine killed at least six people and damaged Kyiv’s Northern Bridge, disrupting traffic for a third day in Moscow’s latest effort to complicate life in the Ukrainian capital. Previously, it has hit apartment blocks, supermarket warehouses, gas stations, datacentres and other civilian targets.
- A continuing Ukrainian counteroffensive dubbed Vivaldi had recaptured about 140 sq km (54 sq miles) of Ukraine’s eastern Donbas region, Zelenskyy told Reuters. It is a setback for Putin who wants Russia to completely control the Donbas before agreeing to any peace deal. Zelenskyy said Ukraine was working to offset low supplies of ammunition for its fighter aircraft – F-16s and MiGs – that bring down about 60% of the Russian jet-powered drones. He said Ukraine was working to boost its jamming capabilities; and in the second half of October it would receive a first shipment of small, cheap air defence missiles capable of hitting new jet-powered Shahed drones. Ukraine had begun to deploy its own domestically made ballistic missile – the FP-7, which has a range of about 250km (155 miles), said Zelenskyy. It hoped to have a longer-range model, the FP-9, ready by autumn.
- Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, arrived in Kyiv on Sunday accompanied by CEOs from German defence companies in a show of support for Volodymyr Zelenskyy amid increased Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities. “I travelled to Kyiv today because Ukraine needs all our support in the coming weeks,” Merz said, saying that Russian forces were bombings towns, residential buildings and heating plants. “If Russia is not stopped, sooner or later its war machine will turn against us … I will tell President Zelenskyy today: you can continue to count on our help.”
- Exit polls from Latvia’s parliamentary election published on Saturday night favoured prime minister Andris Kulbergs’s centrist, pro-Ukraine United List party, suggesting the country will maintain its pro-European and pro-Ukrainian course. But populist parties also had a good night after an election campaign dominated by fears about neighbouring Russia and the cost of living at home. With 72% of ballots counted, United List was on 36.5%, followed by the populist, Maga-style Latvia First on 13.0%. Kulbergs told journalists his party would not cooperate with any parties that were pro-Russian: “Our strong position is that any economic ties with Russia makes us weak; Russia would exploit this.”
- Baltic countries have warned for months that Russia is mounting sabotage, cyber and other hybrid attacks across Europe to erode support for Ukraine and sow fear, although some western officials doubt it is capable of launching a direct assault on Nato, of which Latvia is a member. Throughout his campaign, Kulbergs promised more anti-drone capabilities for Latvia and to maintain defence spending at 5% of gross domestic product, one of the highest levels in Nato. His pro-Kremlin rivals said Latvia should stop any aid to Ukraine and instead focus more on cost-of-living issues, particularly among the country’s Russian-speaking minority.

articles.title: Long-Range FP-9 Missile Ready This Fall, Zelensky Says
articles.body:
Ukraine’s domestically developed FP-9 ballistic missile, designed to reach targets at distances including Moscow, will be operational this fall, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced in an interview with Reuters.
Zelensky stated that he contacted the leadership of Ukrainian defense manufacturer Fire Point to urge the expedited finalization of the FP-9, following the combat debut earlier in the week of the shorter-range FP-7 tactical ballistic missile.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I told them: where is my FP-9? We need the FP-9. And the FP-9 will be [ready] this autumn, I am confident,” Zelensky said.
The president added that Ukraine plans to intensify precision strikes against Russian oil refineries to counter an expanded aerial campaign by Moscow aimed at forcing residents to evacuate Kyiv and other urban centers ahead of winter.
Citing intelligence documents, Zelensky said Russian President Vladimir Putin approved an operational directive expanding strikes against a wider array of civilian targets, including roads, transportation links, schools, and hospitals.
“We have seen the documents and we know that they permit attacks on infrastructure, logistics, roads, schools, hospitals to force people to leave the capital, to leave different cities. This is the goal of the operation,” Zelensky said, attributing the shift in Russian tactics to frontline pressures and personnel losses in the Donbas.

Zelensky emphasized that while Ukraine will respond to Moscow’s attacks on its energy grid by targeting Russian energy infrastructure, Ukrainian forces will not conduct indiscriminate attacks on civilian sites.
“We must react in any possible way. To their attacks on our energy sector, we must respond with strikes against their energy sector. Above all – on oil refineries: that is what provides them money for this war. But we will certainly not, as they do, strike any civilian facilities,” Zelensky said.
Deep-strike operations and overnight engagements
Zelensky confirmed that Ukrainian forces carried out long-range strikes early Saturday morning, Oct. 3.
According to the president, the overnight strikes engaged Russian Iskander missile launcher positions and personnel in the Bryansk region alongside targets in the Samara region.
“Over the past 24 hours, our long-range capability worked effectively against facilities operating for the aggressor’s war machine,” Zelensky stated on social media, adding that Ukrainian operations also produced new results in the Black Sea, without disclosing operational specifics.
The confirmed strikes follow an ongoing campaign by Ukrainian defense forces targeting rear logistics, air surveillance networks, and missile batteries deployed in Russian border regions.
Fire Point development and the FREYJA initiative
The deployment timeline for the FP-9 follows Ukraine’s first operational combat use of the FP-7 tactical ballistic missile on Thursday, Oct. 1.
Manufactured by Fire Point, the baseline FP-7 carries a 150-kilogram warhead across an operational reach of approximately 200 to 250 kilometers.
Fire Point founder and chief designer Denys Shtilerman previously compared the platform to the US-manufactured Army Tactical Missile System (ATACMS), noting that the sovereign weapon is produced at roughly half the acquisition cost with domestic manufacturing spanning rocket motors and flight guidance systems.
Fire Point officially announced the development of both the FP-7 and the longer-range FP-9 in September 2025, conducting initial flight trials of the FP-7 in February 2026.
Prior to its combat deployment, Fire Point Chief Executive Officer Iryna Terekh confirmed that the FP-7 had completed roughly 15 test launches and final Defense Ministry certifications.
The defense contractor also serves as the industrial hub for the European FREYJA initiative, launched in July alongside nine partner nations to build low-cost ballistic missile interceptors.
Under that program, Fire Point is developing the FP-7.X high-speed interceptor variant, aiming for unit production costs below €1 million ($1.2 million) to reduce reliance on scarce US-supplied Patriot batteries ahead of planned operational interception trials in 2027.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Germany’s Merz pledges €1bn in military aid to Kyiv as Russia ramps up attacks
articles.body:
- Germany won’t be intimidated into dropping its support for Ukraine, chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Sunday as he announced €1bn ($1.1bn) in military aid during a visit to Kyiv. Merz said Germany would fund the joint production of drones designed to intercept Russia’s jet-powered drones, adding that “significant technical breakthroughs” in recent weeks were speeding up production. Speaking alongside Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Merz also announced €350m for repairs to the energy sector.
- German officials said company executives who travelled with Merz had signed 14 agreements with Ukraine worth about €6.6bn. They included an agreement with Germany’s Diehl Defence for the supply of IRIS-T air defence missiles, as well as a deal for radar equipment with Hensoldt and for jet drone interceptors with Quantum Systems.
- Air raid sirens and explosions rang out repeatedly across the Ukrainian capital during the German chancellor’s visit. A Russian drone hit Kyiv’s key Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River, marking the fourth consecutive day that Russia has targeted bridges used by tens of thousands of residents commuting between the city’s two banks. Video footage showed cars driving across the bridge as the drone plunged into the roadway and exploded in a burst of fire. Later on Sunday, a Russian airstrike hit Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-biggest city, killing one person and injured another six, mayor Ihor Terekhov said on Telegram.
- In Kyiv, Merz said Germany’s financial help was not only about protecting Ukraine’s territorial integrity. “We do it deeply in our own interest, for it is a matter of Europe’s security,” he said, adding that Russia was carrying out cyber-attacks and disinformation campaigns targeting European democracy. Russia has said accusations of hybrid warfare are baseless and the result of anti-Russian hysteria.
- Zelenskyy said on Sunday he believed Russia might have shared jet-drone technology with its ally North Korea. Earlier in the war, North Korea supplied Russia with millions of artillery shells, and it has since provided ballistic missiles that Moscow regularly uses to attack Ukrainian cities. Asked if Russia had shared with North Korea the technology behind its latest generation of jet-powered drones, Zelenskyy told journalists: “They [Russia] are sharing with North Korea all the technologies. I don’t know about the ballistic and etc but I think yes, because North Korea helped them with missiles.”
- Meanwhile, Ukraine’s military has again used drones to deliver food and medicine to the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine,  foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said on Sunday. Oleshky, a frontline town on the Dnipro River, which separates Russian and Ukrainian forces, has become “a hell on earth” under Russian occupation since 2022, according to residents. Sybiha, who has previously accused Russia of starving residents, said the latest delivery contained almost four metric tons of food and medicine. Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said last month that Russia had not agreed to Ukrainian proposals to allow civilians to evacuate.
- As Zelenskyy on Sunday said the US wanted to hold a new round of peace talks with Ukraine and Russia by the end of October, India said it was seeking a greater role in brokering an end to the war, the foreign minister said. Subrahmanyam Jaishankar said at a Munich Security Conference in New Delhi on Sunday that India had been advocating for a peace deal “for many years, and in recent months we have got a little bit more involved beyond advocacy, so we have conversations with both Russia and Ukraine in this regard”. He said India was starting with Black Sea safety of shipping but also including discussions about grain and energy exports and “on non-attack possibilities”.

articles.title: Russia strikes Kyiv bridges with drones as Putin escalates attacks on Ukraine
articles.body:
Russia continued its extensive assault on bridges in the Ukrainian capital Kyiv on Sunday, first-person view (FPV) drones on roads crossing the Dnipro River for a fourth straight day. The bridges connect the eastern and western parts of the city, and the attacks appear aimed at sowing panic among Ukrainians and disrupting supply routes while causing massive traffic jams. At least four air raid alerts sounded in Kyiv Sunday morning, and a Russian drone exploded on the Northern Bridge over the Dnipro as vehicles were crossing it. No injuries have been reported so far in that incident.
Russia began attacking Kyiv’s bridges on Thursday, saying it was seeking to sever supply routes to the Ukrainian military from central Ukraine to the east. On Thursday and Friday, it repeatedly attacked the city’s Southern Bridge with drones, forcing its closure and causing massive traffic jams across the Kyiv metropolitan area, home to about 3 million people.
The strikes were Russia’s first significant attacks on a major bridge in Kyiv since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. On Saturday, it also attacked the Northern Bridge, which it struck again Sunday. Ukraine has now been forced to partially or fully close three of the six bridges over the Dnipro that carry vehicle traffic, causing severe congestion across large parts of the city throughout the weekend.
Russia is attacking Kyiv’s bridges with domestically produced jet-powered drones, which it has increasingly deployed in recent weeks. The drones are fast and relatively inexpensive, and their speed makes them more difficult for Ukrainian air defense systems to intercept. Russia has used them to strike not only bridges but also residential buildings, supermarket warehouses, gas stations and server farms.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky acknowledged in an interview with Reuters on Saturday that his country is managing to intercept only about 60% of the drones and has been forced to rely heavily on its F-16 and MiG fighter jets, whose ammunition stocks are running low. He said Kyiv is urgently seeking other solutions, including upgrades to its electronic jamming capabilities. Ukraine is expected to receive its first shipment of small, inexpensive air defense missiles capable of striking the new drones in the second half of October.
Russia describes its broad assault on Ukraine in recent days as a campaign of retaliation. On Saturday, it urged diplomats and foreign nationals in Kyiv to leave the city ahead of further “mass retaliatory strikes,” which it said would target military sites in Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities. Russia says it is seeking to make Ukraine pay for its repeated drone attacks in recent months against oil refineries and storage facilities deep inside Russia, strikes that caused a Russian fuel crisis over the summer, as well as attacks on warehouses belonging to Russian e-commerce giants Wildberries and Ozon, which caused significant disruptions for Russian consumers. The strikes on Russian refineries have also repeatedly drawn criticism from U.S. President Donald Trump, who argues that they are worsening the global diesel shortage.
Zelensky defies Trump: We will double attacks on oil refineries
Russia’s retaliatory attacks in recent weeks have included almost daily drone strikes. On Friday, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko described the situation in the capital as “extremely dramatic,” saying Moscow was “destroying” the city by systematically targeting its infrastructure and logistics. Nevertheless, Zelensky said in his Reuters interview Saturday that the Ukrainian military would double its attacks on oil refineries in Russia.
Zelensky said Ukrainian intelligence services had obtained documents indicating that Russian President Vladimir Putin had formulated a “new doctrine” for military attacks against a far broader range of civilian targets ahead of the coming winter. According to Zelensky, the doctrine is intended to pressure Ukrainians to leave the capital and other cities. Zelensky attributed the shift to what he described as Putin’s battlefield setbacks, particularly in “Operation Vivaldi,” in which he said Ukraine recaptured about 140 square kilometers (54 square miles) of territory in the eastern Donbas region that had previously been seized by Russia.
Despite Russia’s call Saturday for diplomats to leave Kyiv, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in the Ukrainian capital Sunday morning. Merz traveled to Kyiv by train and was greeted upon stepping off the train by Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha. The chancellor said he had come to demonstrate his support for Ukraine because it “needs all our support in the coming weeks.” He warned: “If Russia is not stopped, sooner or later its war machine will be turned against us.”
Merz, whose country is among Ukraine’s largest supporters in its war against Russia, arrived in Kyiv accompanied by Economy Minister Katherina Reiche and senior business executives. He is expected to announce a new military aid package for Ukraine worth about 1 billion euros, specifically intended to help counter Russia’s jet-powered drones. He is also expected to pledge 350 million euros in assistance for Ukrainian infrastructure ahead of winter, a critical period in which Ukraine fears massive Russian attacks on its power plants, similar to those in 2025 that repeatedly left millions of people without electricity or heating in freezing temperatures.
Merz, who is deeply unpopular at home, arrives in Ukraine after stinging defeats in regional elections to the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which advocates ending aid to Kyiv and normalizing relations with Moscow. Polls show that nationwide, the AfD is currently Germany’s most popular party.

articles.title: Japan’s island-defense glide missile seen at Camp Fuji
articles.body:
- New video shows Japan's Type 25 Hyper Velocity Gliding Projectile launcher arriving, raising into firing position and withdrawing at Camp Fuji.
- Japan deployed the missile to Camp Fuji on March 31 and plans new units in Hokkaido and Kyushu during fiscal 2026.
New video from Camp Fuji shows Japan’s Type 25 Hyper Velocity Gliding Projectile launcher driving onto a firing site, raising its missiles into launch position and packing up again, giving a rare look at how the country’s first domestically built long-range strike missile is operated.
The three-minute clip was posted on X by Japanese military photographer @yahou5, who described it as the full sequence from arrival through moving into firing posture to withdrawal. It shows a heavy 8×8 truck carrying two large missile canisters on its back. The post was tagged with Camp Fuji and the Japan Ground Self-Defense Force’s Fuji School, which runs the service’s artillery training.
Japan deployed the weapon to Camp Fuji in Shizuoka Prefecture on March 31, the same day the Defense Ministry gave it its official name. Developed as the Hyper Velocity Gliding Projectile for island defense, it was redesignated the Type 25 HVGP, also known as 25HGP. The unit at Camp Fuji is the Field Artillery Training Unit, which is using the first systems to train crews and work out how the weapon will be used.
Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said at the time that the deployment, together with the Type 25 surface-to-ship missile sent to Camp Kengun in Kumamoto, was the first time domestically produced stand-off missiles had been delivered to Japanese military units. Stand-off weapons are meant to hit an enemy force from outside the range of its own weapons.
The HVGP works differently from a cruise missile. A rocket booster carries it to high altitude, where the warhead section separates and glides toward the target at very high speed, maneuvering on the way down. That combination of speed and an unpredictable flight path makes it harder to intercept than a conventional ballistic missile. Japanese outlet Jiji Press has described it as a type of hypersonic glide weapon, flying at more than five times the speed of sound.
The Defense Ministry says the current Block 1 version has a range of several hundred kilometers. Japanese media have reported figures of up to 900 km (560 miles). The ministry is developing longer-range versions, with a goal of 1,000 to 2,000 km, and a later Block 2 with a more advanced glide body is planned for the 2030s.
The launcher made its first public appearance at the Fuji Firepower Review, Japan’s largest annual live-fire demonstration, at the East Fuji Maneuver Area on June 7. There, it raised its two launch tubes upright to show its firing posture. No missile was fired.
Camp Fuji is only the first stop. The Defense Ministry plans to form new HVGP units at Camp Kamifurano in Hokkaido and Camp Ebino in Miyazaki Prefecture on Kyushu during fiscal 2026, which ends in March 2027.
The deployment has drawn attention from local officials. The ministry told the town of Oyama, home to Camp Fuji, that launch equipment would be stationed there, but it has declined to say whether warheads are kept at the base.

articles.title: Ukraine to Deploy Small Missiles, Turrets Against Jet Drones, Zelensky Says
articles.body:
Ukraine will begin deploying domestically produced small missiles by late October to counter Russian jet-powered strike drones, alongside expanding networks of automated gun turrets around the capital region, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced during a joint press briefing with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Kyiv on Sunday, Oct. 4.
According to Ukringrom, Zelensky confirmed that Ukrainian defense enterprises have developed several types of specialized, lower-cost interceptor missiles engineered to neutralize high-speed unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), with initial combat deployments anticipated during the second half of the month.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The small missile program – I will not state the name now, there are several types – we will evidently see results in the second half of this month. We expect to see results,” Zelensky said.
While the missiles are not yet in serial mass production, the president stated that manufacturing can be scaled up rapidly once operational performance is confirmed.
Zelensky noted that Ukrainian forces currently intercept roughly 50 to 60 percent of incoming turbojet Shahed drones, with combat aviation demonstrating the highest efficacy against high-velocity targets.
“Right now, high-quality interception of [jet UAVs] is about 50 percent, 55 percent, sometimes 60 percent – that is our aviation,” Zelensky said.
“F-16s are helping very significantly, and 20mm ammunition is working well.”
Germany Pledges €1.3B Defense Package During Merz Kyiv Visit
Automated defensive turrets in Kyiv
To reinforce ground-level interception networks, Zelensky announced that Ukrainian defense units have installed more than 12 automated counter-drone turrets across the capital, with plans to deploy eight additional systems in the surrounding Kyiv region.
The automated modules are configured to fire 50-caliber (12.7mm) ammunition to destroy incoming loitering munitions on terminal approach vectors. Zelensky explained that the installations form part of a layered, combined defense posture required to address Moscow’s evolving air assault doctrine.
“The Russians will now focus precisely on jet-powered drones and ballistics,” Zelensky observed. “Regarding mass strikes similar to what we are seeing now, I believe they will move toward quality rather than quantity, transitioning from conventional Shaheds to maximum utilization of jet variants.”
The technological adaptation arrives as Russian forces have increasingly paired high-speed loitering munitions with ballistic missile salvos to overwhelm mobile air defense fire teams and deplete inventories of high-end surface-to-air guided missiles.
Bilateral drone agreement
The technical announcements coincided with the formal conclusion of a bilateral agreement between Ukraine and Germany to deepen operational cooperation in counter-drone warfare, enabling German defense manufacturers to integrate Ukrainian combat lessons directly into joint production ventures.
Chancellor Merz emphasized that defense cooperation between Berlin and Kyiv functions as a reciprocal partnership, noting that German corporate representatives accompanying his delegation are studying Ukrainian battlefield adaptations while establishing joint high-tech industrial facilities.
Merz referenced a thwarted Russian-directed sabotage plot at Leipzig/Halle Airport on Aug. 4 as a clear demonstration of why counter-drone technologies are critical for Germany’s own domestic security.
Addressing Russian rhetoric, Merz stated that public threats issued by the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs warning foreign diplomats of “mortal danger” in Kyiv did not influence his decision to visit the Ukrainian capital.
“Despite the threats that reached us from Moscow in recent days, I came today. Together with me came a colleague from the government, Federal Minister for Economic Affairs Katharina Reiche, a large delegation from my government, and a major economic delegation,” Merz said.
“This shows: we will not allow ourselves to be intimidated.”
The chancellor added that ongoing Russian drone attacks on the capital during his visit underscored Moscow’s conduct, reaffirming that Berlin’s solidarity remains steadfast on his second visit to Kyiv as head of government and fourth overall.
Diplomatic resilience
Merz’s presence in Kyiv follows public assurances from EU Ambassador to Ukraine Katarína Mathernová, who confirmed that no EU member state embassy is preparing to evacuate the capital despite Moscow’s threats and infrastructure strikes.
Mathernová confirmed regular coordination with the diplomatic missions of 25 EU member states based in Kyiv, stating that both the EU Delegation and the EU Advisory Mission (EUAM) Ukraine remain fully operational.
The ambassador characterized Moscow’s escalatory statements as an attempt to compensate for military setbacks on the battlefield, echoing statements by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine that standard diplomatic protocols mandate prior notification and that zero relocation requests have been received.

articles.title: Merz unveils new aid for Ukraine as Russia strikes Kyiv during German leader's visit
articles.body:
Merz unveils new aid for Ukraine as Russia strikes Kyiv during German leader's visit
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced a new aid package for Ukraine worth more than 1.3 billion euros ($1.5 billion) during a visit to Kyiv on Sunday marked by renewed Russian attacks on the Ukrainian capital, including the latest drone attack on a bridge spanning the Dnipro River.

Ukraine and Germany have signed a €1.3-billion deal to help fight the surge in Russian drone attacks, while renewed strikes and air raid sirens greeted Chancellor Friedrich Merz on a solidarity visit Sunday.
The agreement worth more than 1.3 billion euros includes some 1 billion euros for weapons including combat drones, while 350 billion euros goes towards supporting Ukraine's battered energy sector, which Russia is targeting to cut off heating and power during the freezing winter months.
As the two met, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Washington had proposed fresh talks with both Ukraine and Russia by the end of the month.
Merz, on a surprise visit to show European support as attacks increase, discovered the new reality of daily life in the Ukrainian capital.
Air raid sirens wailed repeatedly, including as Zelensky showed him the damage to the National Academy of Sciences, which was hit by a Russian attack drone on Monday, killing two.
"We can see the entire pointlessness of this war at this place," noted Merz.
"These barbarous attacks on the civilian population of Ukraine must stop. These are war crimes that are being committed daily here."

One blast that was heard across the city damaged the road surface of the Northern Bridge – one of several connecting the eastern and western parts of Kyiv over the Dnipro river, which have been struck repeatedly in the last four days.
Round-the-clock attacks
Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko has said the capital – largely spared from the devastation wrought near the front line in more than four years of conflict – should now be on a war footing.
Round-the-clock attacks have hit residential areas, petrol stations, schools, rail and communications infrastructure, while the near-constant air raid sirens disrupt daily life and put people on edge.
Watch morePutin's war for the history books: Dmytro Kuleba speaks to FRANCE 24
As he arrived, Merz said that support for Ukraine was vital for European security.
"If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us," he claimed.
Ukraine has repeatedly called for advanced interceptors to shoot down Russia's new fast-moving, jet-powered drones and powerful ballistic missiles.
The latest deal provides for the joint production of anti-jet drones, Merz told a joint news conference with Zelensky.
"Significant technical breakthroughs have already been achieved in this area in recent weeks," he added.
"Production is now being ramped up. This strengthens Ukrainian air defence quickly and significantly.
"We are supplying standoff weapons, combat drones and satellite technology so that Ukraine can also target Russian launch sites."
Military support
Talks to end Europe's worst conflict since World War II have been at a standstill and both sides have promised to ramp up long-range attacks on military and related targets.
But Zelensky said Sunday that the United States was proposing "technical level" talks with both sides by the end of this month, possibly including UAE mediators.
"We respond positively to negotiations," he added.
Merz called this week for NATO and European unity against Russia, as well as in his own country, where the far-right, Moscow-friendly AfD opposition is on the rise.
There have been increasing fears in Europe that it could find itself in Russia's crosshairs.
Security was a top concern for voters in this weekend's election in NATO member Latvia, which borders Russia.
Read moreLatvia's PM on track to lead pro-Ukraine coalition after parliamentary election victory
On Saturday, Moscow warned foreigners and diplomats to leave Kyiv, saying "massive" new airstrikes would hit the city.
Leaders from countries allied to Ukraine have continued to make visits despite a similar threat made in May.
"The EU Delegation is staying," European Union ambassador Katarina Mathernova wrote on X on Sunday.
"Threatening us will not stop Europe's support for Ukraine," she added. "It only reminds us why that support matters!"
Merz told reporters he was unfazed by the threat but did not know if it had been made to coincide with his visit.
In Kyiv, home to some three million people, residents are mulling what to do if that happens again, and there have been calls for the vulnerable and disabled to consider leaving.
Merz said Berlin's winter support programme will help provide generators, transformer stations and for grid repairs.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: Iran FM says war has no military solution, Trump mulls strikes
articles.body:
The live blog has now closed and will be back tomorrow. You can read more of The New Arab's coverage of the war in the Middle East here.
Breadcrumb
The New Arab's live coverage of the war in the region has now closed. Here were the top stories:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered a security review of international flights to Israel on Sunday, after an attempt by an Omani co-pilot to crash an Israel-bound flight from Dubai.
Netanyahu "has instructed the Head of the National Security Council, Shmuel Ben Ezra, to appoint an examiner to conduct a thorough review of all security aspects of foreign civil aviation to Israel", a statement from the premier's office said.
A committee of the Mecca defence pact between Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan will hold talks in Riyadh on Monday, with Turkish ministers among those attending, the Turkish foreign ministry said on Sunday.
The leader of Yemen's Saudi-backed government announced on Sunday the beginning of a major military operation against the Iran-backed Houthis earlier on Sunday, aimed at seizing the territory under their control.
Pakistan's foreign minister said on Friday that Iran had suggested engaging Yemen's Houthis politically after attacks by the group, an idea that the Mecca defence pact committee would discuss at a meeting in Riyadh this week.
"The meeting will address recent developments in the region and the stage reached in the Alliance’s institutionalisation efforts," the Turkish statement said.
It said Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, Defence Minister Yasar Guler and chief of the general staff General Selcuk Bayraktaroglu would attend the meeting of the pact's strategic political and defence committee, along with officials from Pakistan and Saudi Arabia.
The Green Party in the UK has passed a motion with 1,022 votes in favour and 813 against defining Zionism as "an ethnonationalist political project."
"The Green Party is an anti-racist party and has consistently opposed the illegal occupation of both Palestinian and Syrian land, called for an end to arms sales to the Israeli government, and spoken out fearlessly about the devastating situation in Gaza and the West Bank," a spokesperson for the party said, according to Al Jazeera.
You can read more about the motion here:
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi called for "dialogue, not confrontation" over Africa's cross-border disputes on Sunday, as he prepared to meet three leaders whose countries share increasingly strained relations with Ethiopia.
Sisi was due to hold talks at El Alamein with Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki, Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud and Sudanese army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, alongside an African Union summit hosted by Egypt.
The Egyptian presidency says the four-way meeting is intended for "consultation and coordination on regional issues of mutual interest".
But the gathering comes amid renewed war in northern Ethiopia and rapidly deteriorating relations between Addis Ababa and several of the countries attending, raising questions over whether an informal anti-Ethiopia alignment is emerging in the Horn of Africa.
Iranian airlines resumed flights to Iraq's Najaf on Sunday after the United States granted Baghdad an exemption allowing sanctioned Iranian carriers to operate to the city holy to Shia Muslims, an AFP correspondent said.
Najaf airport official Hussein Muhanna told AFP that "flights between Iraq and the Islamic Republic of Iran have resumed via Najaf International Airport."
The first flight was operated by Caspian Airlines with AFP's correspondent at the airport reporting seeing the plane land at 5:15 pm (1415 GMT).
On Friday, the Iraqi government said it had secured an agreement with the US allowing Iranian airlines, except Mahan Air, to operate 40 daily flights to and from Najaf, which is home to one of the most revered shrines in Shia Islam.
Last month, Iraq enforced the US ban on Iranian carriers, leaving travellers scrambling for solutions, especially at Najaf's airport, which is a major hub for Iranian flights and their main destination in Iraq.
The Saudi government is providing $59.7m to Yemen's government, according to the Saudi Press Agency, which quoted a statement saying, "This will stimulate economic and social development towards a more sustainable path, and will positively impact purchasing power, ensure stable incomes for families, and revitalise commercial markets."
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said they launched ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi Aramco sites in Riyadh and the Khurais area, claiming the attacks caused major fires, in response to what they said were 50 Saudi-led coalition air and missile strikes in Yemen over the past 12 hours.
The leader of Yemen's Saudi-backed government announced the beginning of a major military operation against the Iran-backed Houthis on Sunday, aimed at seizing the territory under their control.
Regional and Western officials had previously told Reuters that Saudi Arabia and its Yemeni allies were planning to launch an assault on the Houthis, with the Saudis leading aerial combat and Yemeni forces fighting on the ground.
"Today, I announce the start of military operations to retake the remaining territory of the republic and extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory," Yemeni President Rashad al-Alimi said in a televised address.
Yemen's Houthis on Sunday cut a vital supply route linking Taiz with Aden -- the interim capital of the internationally recognised government -- according to four security sources.
"We were informed that the Houthis had taken control of the al-Safiya area, where they cut the main road and took control of the police station," a police source in the area told AFP.
Three sources with the Yemeni military confirmed Houthi control over the area and supply route, with the group effectively encircling Taiz city.
An Israeli airstrike has killed a Palestinian in the city of Khan Younis in Gaza, according to Palestinian news agency Wafa, which added that another person was seriously injured in the strike.
Iran will upgrade the range of its missiles following the war with the US as American forces are now positioned as much as 1,000 km (621 miles) away from the Iranian coast, Army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia told Fars news on Sunday.
"During this war, we concluded that we absolutely must increase the range of our missiles, and we have now moved in that direction," he said.
In late September, Israeli troops raided the Tulkarem area and posted notices on the Banat Yaqub shrine in Irtah, south of the city.
The two-story building, with its Roman-era lower floor and Mamluk-era prayer room above, would now be under the control of the Israel Antiquities Authority.
The shrine and its grounds cover no more than 300 square meters, according to Suhail Salman of the Popular Campaign Against the Wall and Settlements, a Palestinian grassroots group, yet the notices claimed more than 10 dunams (about 2.5 acres) of surrounding land, taking in dozens of inhabited homes.
The shrine is the latest site in a campaign that uses heritage protection to seize land and override Palestinian jurisdiction, rights groups and archaeologists say.
From Silwan in East Jerusalem to Shiloh, Tel Rumeida in Hebron, and Sebastia near Nablus, excavations have arrived alongside roads, visitor centres, and restrictions on access that turn Palestinian land into settler-run tourist sites.
Iraq's state-owned Oil Tanker Company transported 2 million barrels of Iraqi crude aboard a very large crude carrier (VLCC) through the Strait of Hormuz, in what its director general described on Saturday as the company's first such operation in decades.
The announcement means the company is transporting the crude through the strait rather than delivering it at the port of Basra, giving state oil marketer SOMO greater flexibility in how and where it sells the crude.
The company's director general, Ali Qais Abdul Jabbar, said in a statement that the move could allow SOMO to take advantage of better sales and pricing opportunities.
Iraq's Oil Tanker Company is also working to buy and own specialised crude oil tankers to expand its fleet and strengthen its ability to compete with regional shipping companies, he added.
Iraq has previously secured Iranian permission for Iraqi oil tankers to transit the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran has effectively closed during its conflict with the US.
A tanker was hit by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz, causing damage to its engine room, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said on Sunday, without specifying when the incident occurred.
The crew was safe and no environmental impact had been reported at the time the notice was issued, UKMTO added.

Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that there is no military solution to his country's conflict with the United States, with talks on ending the war apparently at an impasse.
"If our enemies again choose the path of military confrontation, our response will be stronger than before, and we will defend ourselves with even more force," Araghchi said at a gathering of foreign ambassadors. "There is no military solution, nor any solution based on new sanctions."
The US aircraft carrier George H.W. Bush arrived in Thailand's resort island of Phuket on Sunday with about 4,800 personnel aboard for a rest-and-recreation break after six months supporting US operations in the Middle East.
For the last six months, the Nimitz-class aircraft carrier and its strike group supported Operation Epic Fury and the US naval blockade in the US Central Command area of responsibility to secure maritime security and stability in the Middle East, according to the US Navy.
Phuket is the first port call for the George H.W. Bush Carrier Strike Group since departing Norfolk, Virginia, and Mayport, Florida, in March, the US Navy said in a statement.
The Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until seven Iranian conditions set out in a June interim agreement with the US are met, Nournews reported Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf as saying on Sunday, a few days after Tehran received Washington's reply to its diplomatic proposal.
“The Americans, who say something different in the media, have recently put forward proposals through a mediator. But they must understand that the period of dragging out the process and dictating one-sided demands is over," Ghalibaf was quoted as saying.
"The position of the Islamic Republic of Iran is completely clear and firm, and the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened until our seven conditions, based on the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, are met."

articles.title: Defense Forces Hit Kaluga Radio Tube Plant Producing Components for Kh-101 and Iskander-M
articles.body:
The Defense Forces of Ukraine hit Voskhod-KLRZ, also known as the Kaluga Radio Tube Plant. This electronics manufacturer produces components for Kh-101 and Iskander-K cruise missiles, as well as Iskander-M ballistic missiles.
The OSINT project Supernova+ reported this on the evening of October 3, citing local residents.
Judging by videos published by local residents, cruise missiles or jet-powered drones were used in the strike. A characteristic jet-engine sound can be heard before the explosion.
Meanwhile, the governor claimed that Russian forces had destroyed 13 UAVs over the Kaluga region and Kaluga itself.
The Varta OSINT project reported that the Voskhod JSC, or the Kaluga Radio Tube Plant, specializes in developing and manufacturing high-reliability microelectronics, semiconductor components, specialized materials for the electronics industry, and equipment for testing components.
The plant produces digital integrated circuits, operational amplifiers, transistor arrays, optocouplers, semiconductor lasers and photodiodes. In a 2012 presentation, the company stated that more than 90% of its products were intended for Russia’s defense industry.
According to Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence, Voskhod is involved in producing Kh-101 cruise missiles. The company manufactured OSM140UD17A and UD601A operational amplifiers for the K003 computing unit, as well as 544UD16U3 amplifiers and N590KN13 analog switches for the Monoblock-L unit.
For the 9M727 missile of the Iskander-K system, the plant supplies trunk transmitters for the Zarya-61M onboard computer. It also manufactures converters, operational amplifiers, logic elements, and analog switches for circuit boards of the GIB-123-4 inertial navigation system.
The company is also involved in the production of 9M723 ballistic missiles of the Iskander-M system. According to Ukrainian intelligence, Voskhod manufactures and supplies RUD20 microchips for these missiles.
Another military-related area of the plant’s work is equipment for maintaining armored vehicles. Its catalog includes the UChS-1G system for chemical cleaning of 125mm tank gun barrels and the PPSG-2-2 device for testing generator systems of BMP-2 and BMP-3 infantry fighting vehicles, as well as the starter-generator system of the T-72 tank. The company’s public catalog also offers the PKV-003 device for crimping, or mechanically securing, fuzes screwed into artillery ammunition ranging from 37mm to 152mm in caliber.
Ukraine imposed sanctions on Voskhod under Decree No. 227/2023 dated April 15, 2023, for a period of 10 years. At the same time, the company is not subject to sanctions imposed by the United States, the European Union, or the United Kingdom.
In early September, it was reported that almost half of the 155 companies owned by the Russian Roselectronika industrial holding, which specializes in developing and manufacturing radio-electronic components, remain outside sanctions.
