articles.title: US prepares to deploy extra troops and aircraft to Israel: report
articles.body:
The United States has prepared to deploy additional troops and aircraft to Israel over the coming weeks, Israeli media reported, as Washington and Tel Aviv brace for a potential military escalation across the Middle East as per media reports.
According to Israeli news outlet Walla, citing security sources, roughly 3,000 US personnel are currently stationed across Israel.
Their roles include operating air defence missile batteries, conducting flight operations, providing logistical support, and serving as direct liaisons at military headquarters.
Whilst routine unit rotations have occurred in recent weeks, defence officials confirmed that fresh personnel and combat aircraft will arrive shortly to reinforce existing capabilities.
A senior Israeli security official told Walla that regional adversaries are closely monitoring elections in Israel and the US, evaluating ways to destabilise the regional balance without triggering outright conflict.
"They understand that the Israeli response this time will be extremely aggressive," the official warned.
CENTCOM coordination
Operational planning between the Israel Defence Forces and US Central Command (CENTCOM) remains focused on potential retaliatory strikes and targets inside Iran in the event of renewed ballistic missile launches.
The military build-up follows diplomatic overtures by Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, who reiterated to envoys in Tehran that Iran remains open to diplomatic settlements.
In late September, Tehran relayed seven conditions via Qatari mediation for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which US President Donald Trump rejected.
Concurrently, Israeli security officials assess that ongoing fighting against Yemen's Houthi movement could reshape Gulf security partnerships, citing increased cooperation between Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.
A senior official warned that regional actors failing to confront Houthi forces immediately risk facing subsequent attacks alone.
Hostilities in Yemen have flared following Houthi advances across Al Hudaydah and Taiz provinces, including the capture of Mokha and strategic positions on Mayun Island overseeing the Bab al Mandeb Strait, further straining the conflict.

articles.title: Russia strikes data center and logistics hub in Ukraine – MOD (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Russia strikes data center and logistics hub in Ukraine – MOD (VIDEO)
The Russian military has struck a data center and a logistics hub in Ukraine, the Defense Ministry in Moscow said on Sunday.
The ministry said that Geran drones targeted a Nova Poshta logistics center in Chernomorsk and a data center in Odessa. Footage released by the MOD shows direct hits on both facilities. Russia has increasingly targeted Ukrainian data centers in recent strikes, with internet and mobile providers reporting damage and connectivity disruptions.
Additionally, Russian forces struck two dry-cargo vessels carrying military supplies to the port of Odessa, hit a drone command post, destroyed an air-surveillance radar, and struck military-used transport infrastructure, weapons depots, drone storage sites, and positions housing Ukrainian troops and foreign mercenaries across 147 locations. It later added that its forces struck Kiev’s Severny road bridge across the Dnieper, which it said was used to move troops and military cargo.
The ministry also reported that its air defenses downed four guided bombs, three US-made HIMARS rockets, and 1,222 fixed-wing drones over the past 24 hours. The ministry further said Russian forces tightened an encirclement in northeastern Kharkov Region and advanced elsewhere, including in northern and central Dobropolye.
Both Kiev and Moscow have ramped up long-range strikes in recent weeks following Ukraine’s botched “pressure campaign,” which saw Kiev intensify drone attacks on Russian civilian and energy infrastructure amid battlefield setbacks. The attacks hit energy facilities, civilian warehouses and logistics hubs, residential buildings, and resort areas, as well as polling stations during last month’s parliamentary elections.
Russia has retaliated by sharply expanding strikes on Ukraine’s military-industrial facilities, shipping, and key ports handling military-related imports. The campaign has severely disrupted Ukrainian Black Sea shipping and logistics. Moscow maintains that it targets only infrastructure supporting Ukraine’s war effort.
President Vladimir Putin recently warned that Ukraine faces a “catastrophic scenario” after “opening Pandora’s box” by attacking Russian economic and civilian infrastructure, which ultimately failed to alter the course of the conflict. Putin also warned that with its “provocative actions,” Kiev was only hindering a peaceful settlement rather than bringing one closer.
Despite the mounting toll, Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky vowed on Saturday to further intensify strikes on Russian oil facilities. The Russian Defense Ministry responded on Sunday by pledging to step up its own campaign. The ministry said Ukrainians “should blame only the head of the Kiev regime” for any further escalation, adding that his threats meant he “bears full personal and political responsibility for it.”

articles.title: Friedrich Merz begins unannounced Kyiv visit as Russia continues strikes on Ukraine’s capital – Europe live
articles.body:
The education minister says 400- 500 high schools will remain partially or fully shut following a week where riot police clashed with high school students as protests on classroom conditions have spread nationwide.
Lessons will be “totally or partly suspended” given the unrest, says Education Minister Edouard Geffray.
He said 24 schools had been “burned or ransacked” since the start of the movement.
At least 5,000 people, mainly teenagers, have been arrested while dozens of people, including students and teachers, have been injured. Unions are calling on teachers to strike.
The protests began last week in the Paris region, with students staging sit-ins over conditions like overcrowding in classrooms, teacher shortages and dilapidated buildings.
The rallies in some cases have become more violent with protesters wearing masks and setting off fires in the street and vidoes showing police officers using batons on students.
More protests had been scheduled for Tuesday this week, prompting law enforcement this weekend to say the situation had grown “out of control”.
Paris police chief Patrice Faure told students to abandon their school blockades to return to peaceful forms of protest and suggested to parents there was influence from “professional rioters”.
We’ll draw our live coverage to a close for today. For the full story on the deals announced from the German chancellor’s surprise visit to Ukraine, you can read this report from my colleague in Kyiv.
Friedrich Merz arrived in the Ukrainian capital this morning to pledge aid and defence deals to Zelenskyy; his arrival was marked soon after by the Russians striking a key bridge in the city
His visit comes as there are near daily bombardments of the Ukrainian capital by the Kremlin, which has hit now both the Northern and Southern Bridges across the Dnipro River which commuters heavily rely on. Russia has also been hitting gas stations in residential neighbourhoods and government and academia sites.
Germany has become Ukraine’s biggest provider of military aid since Merz entered office in May 2025, surpassing the US as American support has declined.
On Sunday, Merz announced another $1.5bn in aid, over a billion of it going towards military aid including long-range strike weapons, drones and satellite tech to help Ukraine hit Russian launch pads.
In France, the government is keeping up to 500 high schools closed tomorrow amid student protests which have “grown out of control”, say police.
The French Education Minister said 78 teachers and education staff had been wounded in the protests late last week where there were outbursts of violence and masked protesters damaging property and setting fires in the street.
On Sunday, police detained a 16-year-old over the assault of a 59-year-old teacher who had been doused with gasoline and assaulted on the sidelines of a school protest.
But students and some human rights groups have also condemned “brutal” policing tactics from riot squads.
Students have been protesting since mid-September about poor conditions in school including a shortage of teachers, overcrowded classrooms and dilapidated buildings. The protests, which began in Paris, have spread across the country with a national action day last Friday. Organisers have called for more protests on Tuesday.
Some more lines in from Ukraine and the German Chancellor’s visit to Kyiv being marked with another Russian strike on the city’s bridges.
Merz used the visit to announce a new showstopping package of aid to Ukraine worth over $1.5bn. About $1.1bn is military aid including long-range strike weapons, combat drones and satellite tech.
Merz said this was so Ukraine could also target Russian launch pads. Increasingly this year we’ve seen long-range strikes from Ukraine landing deep into the heart of Russia. Ukraine has also targeted oil refineries and infrastructure in St Petersburg and Moscow.
Ukraine and Germany had also signed 15 agreements covering security co-operation as well as weapons production and procurement. They also finalised a deal expanding joint drone defence projects.
Merz said Germany would fund the making of drones aimed at intercepting Russia’s jet-powered drones which have been increasingly used by the Kremlin this year to get through Ukraine’s defences. This was urgently needed to strengthen Ukraine’s air defence, he said.
Zelenskyy said Russia had launched 900 such drones this week alone, of which Ukraine had only been able to intercept half.
Severe rains and flooding in Spain’s Catalonia region has led to the deaths of two people in towns north of Barcelona, local authorities say.
One person died when a wall at a campsite in Tordera collapsed and the other drowned in a flooded garage in Montornes del Valles, emergency services said.
At least one other person is also missing following the torrential rains overnight which trapped people in cars and prompted emergency rescues.
Spain’s Meteorological Office (AEMET) warned of “very heavy or torrential rainfall” in Barcelona and Girona on Sunday, noting the storm would be moving northwards and rain could “exceed 200 mm in 12 hours. Extreme caution is advised.”
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has also uregd residents to “avoid non-essential journeys” and follow directions from emergency services.
78 teachers and school staff injured says French minister
Some more detail from France’s Education Minister Edouard Geffray’s comments earlier where he said 400-500 schools would continue to be closed on Monday, following on from Friday’s shut down.
There are roughly 3,700 high schools, or lycees, across the country.
Geffray said lessons were being suspended because the security situation was still not stable enough following outbursts of violence last week amid mass demonstrations.
He claimed activists had infiltrated the protests, “hijacked it from the students themselves, and engaged in extreme violence”.
“Clearly, this poses a risk to both our staff and our students,” he said, noting that 78 education staff had been wounded – “something we have never seen before”.
“They were deliberately targeted because they were employees of the national education system,” Geffray alleged.
In the southern town of La Ciotat, police detained a 16-year-old on Sunday for the assault of a teacher who was doused in gasoline and attacked on the sidelines of a school protest on Friday.
Meanwhile, organisers have called for the protests to continue on Tuesday saying the government hasn’t properly addressed their concerns, raised just a few weeks into the new school year about overcrowded classes and absent teachers.
Students and some rights groups have condemned the heavy-handed tactics of police, accusing them of brutality in removing students from protests.
Incinerated novels and destroyed warehouses: Russia’s war on Ukrainian books
Charlotte Higgins
My colleague Charlotte Higgins has written today’s Sunday read on Russia’s war on Ukrainian books:
On a Saturday morning in August, Viktor Kruglov, the co-founder and chief executive of the publisher Ranok, was at his headquarters in Kharkiv – the eastern Ukrainian city that, along with Kyiv, is the centre of the country’s publishing and printing industry. Built 15 years ago on the site of a former bread factory, the footprint of the premises is about 10,000 sq metres (107,640ft). Books were stacked 12 metres high on rank after rank of shelves.
Kruglov, along with five senior colleagues, were on the warehouse floor to discuss the approaching school year. The warehouse was holding 628,000 new schoolbooks. “It was the high season of distribution,” he said, “so we were checking all our processes: how to do it more successfully, how to do it in time.”
Russia strikes Kyiv bridge as German chancellor visits Ukraine in show of support

A Russian drone hit Kyiv’s key Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River, marking the fourth consecutive day that Russia has targeted bridges used by thousands of residents commuting between the city’s two banks. In the Bosnian capital, Sarajevo, Ismar Garasljevic, a 51-year-old high school teacher tells Reuters:
“More than 30 years after the war, the situation is still the same; we are talking about nationalism ... The same faces, the same story, constantly.“
There is this feeling of more of the same in the bitter ethno-nationalist politics in Bosnia.
There are multi-ethnic opposition coalitions led by the Social Democratic Party but also the major ethnically-based political parties in the Bosniak SDA, Serb SNSD and Croat HDZ BiH.
They have been the ones in government so far but their differences in central government have blocked progress on measures like transparency laws which are needed for Bosnia to gain EU membership. It secured candidate status in 2022 but has progressed little since then.
Reporter Guy de Launey in Sarajevo also has this report from Bosnia on why so many young people have left the country in the past decade:
One local organisation that tracks emigration estimated that more than 600,000 people had left the country in the decade after the 2013 census, when the official population was 3.5 million.
“If I weren’t optimistic, maybe I would also move out,” said Timur Vilić, a 28-year-old municipal councillor in Sarajevo, who is standing on Sunday for election to the cantonal government. He represents Our Party – a multi-ethnic, non-nationalist, liberal movement that he admits faces a struggle to appeal to voters in a country dominated by ethnonationalist parties.
The problem for Our Party – and other non-nationalist movements – is that the young people who make up their support base are voting with their feet, rather than making their mark on ballot papers.
In theory, Sunday’s vote should be one of the great European festivals of democracy, with the election of no fewer than 14 prime ministers and five presidents. But the plethora of posts on offer reflects a fiendishly complicated system of governance.
The Dayton agreement’s creation of two powerful regional “entities” – with a weaker central government – was intended as a stopgap to ensure peace after the ruinous conflict of the 1990s. Instead, it has perpetuated the divisions in the country. Most Serbs live in the Republika Srpska (RS), while the Federation is home to most of Bosnia’s Croats and Bosniak Muslims. There is no incentive for the ethnonationalist leaders to change that situation – or to appeal to young people who see a brighter future outside the country.
“They don’t want young people to be interested, and young people are not interested in politics,” said Sarah Ćato. The 19-year-old student of political science and international relations is eligible to vote on Sunday for the first time – but she says that her age group feels unseen by the political mainstream.
“Young people don’t know how to vote or who to vote for because nobody’s standing for us,” she said, adding that the reluctance to engage in politics reflects its status as a “taboo subject” after the end of the conflict in 1995. “I think educating youth from middle school on how to be a good citizen should be mandatory.”
In Bosnia, ethno-nationalist politics are at the fore of today’s elections.
Voters are casting ballots today for the country’s three-person multi-ethnic presidency, lawmakers in the national parliament as well as the heads of institutions of Bosnia’s two powerful regional “entities”.
It’s a complicated governance structure – set up in the 1995 peace agreement that ended the preceding three-year civil war.
While Bosnia is one of the poorest countries in Europe after that devasating war, it has remained peaceful.
Still its politics remain divided along ethnic lines between the country’s Bosniaks, who are mainly Muslims, and its Serbs and Croats.
The entities – which are stronger than the central government – was set up to maintain that peace but have largely perpetuated the divison. Most Serbs live in the Republika Srpska (RS), while the Muslim-majority Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina is home to most of Bosnia’s Croats and Bosniak Muslims.
And tensions are rising between the two. Bosnian Serb leaders have pushed for the separation of their entity from the rest of Bosnia, and populist party figures like Russia sympathiser Milorad Dodik, said at a final rally on Friday night that modern Bosnia “is dead” and “doesn’t make any sense”.
Earlier, while visiting the science academy in Kyiv targeted by Russian drones on Monday, Merz decried the “war crime”.
“These barbaric attacks on the civilian population of Ukraine must stop. These are daily war crimes,” the German chancellor said.
The National Academy of Science in Kyiv is just a few hundred meters from the German Embassy.
The German leader also issued a comment to Putin, telling him to “end this senseless war” and that “we are ready to talk”.
Zelensky noted that the strikes on Kyiv had continued even amid the chancellor’s visit.
Pro-Ukraine and EU Latvian PM wins parliamentary vote
In Latvia, the small republic right on Nato’s eastern flank, Prime Minister Andris Kulberg’s centre-right party has won the most support in the country’s parliamentary election.
The vote on Saturday had been dominated by concerns over neighbouring Russia as well as cost-of-living and economic issues- and saw about 51% turnout.
Kulberg’s United List party – which won 42 of the 100 seats in parliament, an unprecedented result- will now go about forming a coalition to govern.
Kulberg became prime minister in May after a political crisis over the handling of stray drones suspected to have come from Ukraine, brought down the governing coalition that was in place.
Kulberg, then in opposition, then secured parliamentary approval to lead a new coalition.
He has vowed to push on with his pro-Ukraine and EU direction. Latvia, a small country with a 1.8 million population, which borders both Russia and Moscow-allied Belarus has always supported Ukraine against Russia’s invasion.

articles.title: Iran says no military solution to war as peace talks with US stall
articles.body:
Iran says no military solution to war as peace talks with US stall
Iran's diplomat said on Sunday there was no military solution to the US war against Iran as peace talks appeared stalled. Washington has scaled back attacks in favour of economic pressure, while Iran's attempted Hormuz blockade remains contentious. A UK maritime agency reported another tanker hit by an unidentified projectile.
Iran's top diplomat insisted on Sunday that there would be no military solution to the United States' war against the Islamic republic, with talks on ending the conflict apparently at an impasse.
A campaign of heavy bombardment failed to bring a decisive close to the war launched by the US and Israel in late February, and Washington in recent weeks has dialled back military operations in favour of economic pressure.
The main point of contention remains Iran's attempt to blockade the Strait of Hormuz, a vital conduit for Gulf oil and gas where a UK maritime agency reported on Sunday another tanker was struck by an unknown projectile.
"If our enemies again choose the path of military confrontation, our response will be stronger than before, and we will defend ourselves with even more force," Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said at a gathering of foreign ambassadors.
"There is no military solution, nor any solution based on new sanctions," he continued, adding "only negotiations based on justice and fairness" could end the conflict.
Read moreG7 members will release 100 million barrels of diesel after US threatens export ban
The two sides agreed a memorandum of understanding in June that spelled out a framework for a permanent resolution, but Iranian attacks on vessels in the Hormuz prompted a return to US military operations.
Iran has sought to impose its control over the vital shipping lane since the start of the war, striking vessels that attempt to transit without its authorisation.
The US has imposed its own counterblockade of Iranian ports, and has also struck vessels it accuses of violating it.
On Sunday, the British maritime security agency UKMTO said a tanker in the Hormuz "reported being struck by an unknown projectile, causing damage to the engine room", though the crew were reported safe and no environmental impact was recorded.
The agency did not specify the date of the incident, the vessel's origin or destination, or whether it was an oil tanker or LNG carrier.
In Iran, oil minister Mohsen Paknejad has resigned, the president's office said on Sunday, as the US maintains a blockade on the country's oil exports.
In a news bulletin on the minister's resignation, state television ran an interview with an official from the Iranian presidential office who said Paknejad initially offered to quit a while ago "due to personal issues" but this was rejected.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian had asked Paknejad to continue in his post but was now accepting his departure as the minister had insisted on leaving, the official added.
Paknejad has been replaced by Hamid Bovard, the chief executive of the National Iranian Oil Company, the presidency said.
Focused on Hormuz
Iranian and US officials last week held indirect talks on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, with Tehran saying it presented seven conditions for reopening the strait.
Iran has demanded, among other things, a ceasefire across the Middle East, the unfreezing of its assets abroad, the lifting of sanctions on its oil sector and an end to the US naval blockade.
Trump, however, rejected the proposal, while leaving the door open both to further talks or renewed military operations.
Read moreIran says it expects US response Tuesday on plan to reopen Strait of Hormuz
Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said Sunday that the US had expressed its views on the proposal and said they were being reviewed.
"The Americans, through intermediaries, have also conveyed their views on this proposal, and these views are currently being examined inside the country through the relevant channels and procedures," he told reporters, according to state news agency IRNA.
"Whenever the final position of the Islamic Republic of Iran is ready, appropriate steps will be taken accordingly. At the same time, the Islamic Republic of Iran is also preparing itself for any other possible scenario."
Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei on Sunday characterised the latest US counterproposal as being "in line with their previous proposals concerning nuclear issues".
"We have clearly indicated that we are focusing on the issue of the Strait of Hormuz," he said, adding that reopening the waterway required "an end to the disruptions to Iranian commercial maritime traffic and the lifting of sanctions".
The United States and Israel have said the war is necessary to prevent Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons -- a goal it has long denied pursuing -- though the focus soon shifted to reopening the Hormuz after its closure sent shockwaves through world energy markets.
The United States has not struck Iran since September 1, but it has recently pursued a fresh military buildup in the region.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: SBU Drones Strike Su-35 and Su-34 Jets at Russian Airfield
articles.body:
Long-range strike drones operated by the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) struck advanced Russian Su-35 and Su-34 combat aircraft alongside an ammunition depot at the Khanskaya military airfield in Russia’s Republic of Adygea early Sunday morning, Oct. 4.
According to an official dispatch from the SBU, operators from the service’s “Alpha” Special Operations Center carried out the overnight strike against the air base, located approximately six kilometers outside the regional capital of Maykop and roughly 500 kilometers from Ukrainian-controlled territory.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The security service confirmed direct hits on an Su-35 multi-role air superiority fighter – one of the Russian Aerospace Forces’ most advanced frontline combat aircraft, carrying an estimated export valuation of $100 million – and an Su-34 fighter-bomber, which serves as Moscow’s primary tactical strike aircraft for launching standoff guided aerial bombs, valued at approximately $50 million.
In addition to targeting the combat aircraft, Ukrainian strike drones detonated an on-site ammunition storage facility within the airfield perimeter.
“Last night, the Security Service of Ukraine successfully attacked the military airfield Khanskaya in the Republic of Adygea, Russian Federation,” the SBU stated. “The distance to the target is about 500 kilometers.”
The operation confirms earlier reports from regional monitoring channels and eyewitnesses in Maykop, who reported drone engine sounds and active Russian air defense fire beginning around 1:00 a.m. local time on Sunday, followed by loud secondary explosions and large blazes visible across the airfield complex.
Ukraine to Deploy Small Missiles, Turrets Against Jet Drones, Zelensky Says
Deep-strike campaign
The Khanskaya facility serves as the permanent home station for the Russian Aerospace Forces’ 272nd Training Aviation Base.
Despite its primary instructional designation, Russian military planners have integrated the installation into active combat logistics, utilizing its runways, hangars, and fuel reservoirs as a dispersed forward staging post to support tactical air units.
Satellite reconnaissance recorded in recent months showed a substantial concentration of military aircraft deployed across the installation, including Su-24 bombers, Su-30, Su-34, and Su-35S multi-role fighters, L-39 jet trainers, Mi-8 transport helicopters, and heavy military cargo planes.
The airfield previously came under Ukrainian deep-strike bombardment in December.
The precision strike against Khanskaya marks the second consecutive night of coordinated Ukrainian operations targeting Russian air assets and unmanned aviation nodes.
Overnight into Saturday, Oct. 3, Ukrainian strike drones struck the Tsymbulovo droneport in Russia’s Oryol region, sparking multiple fires across workshops and launch pads used to deploy turbojet-powered loitering munitions toward Kyiv.

articles.title: UK warships to enter South China Sea despite China protest
articles.body:
Royal Navy patrol ships HMS Spey and HMS Tamar are to enter the South China Sea for a ten-day multinational exercise with Australia, Malaysia, New Zealand and Singapore, continuing a British naval presence in waters where Beijing has repeatedly objected to UK military activity and policy, according to the Royal Navy.
The two Batch 2 River-class offshore patrol vessels will take part in Exercise Bersama Lima 26, the annual tri-service exercise conducted under the Five Power Defence Arrangements, or FPDA, which links the United Kingdom with Australia, Malaysia, New Zealand and Singapore.
Bersama Lima, meaning “Together Five” in Malay, will involve ships, aircraft and troops operating across maritime, land and air scenarios. Forces committed to the exercise include frigates, patrol vessels, a corvette, tanker and submarine, as well as divers and specialist boarding teams.
Australian F-35A Lightning II fighters will lead the air element of the exercise, while planned scenarios include troops directing naval gunfire, boarding and searching vessels at sea, anti-submarine warfare and naval air defence supported by participating air forces.
The deployment takes place against a long-running dispute between Beijing and several regional governments over territorial and maritime claims in the South China Sea, as well as wider disagreements over the activities of military forces from countries outside the region. China has repeatedly criticised British involvement. In 2018, Beijing said it had lodged stern representations with the UK after HMS Albion sailed close to the Paracel Islands, which China calls the Xisha Islands. China said the ship had entered waters it regarded as its territorial sea without permission, while Britain has consistently maintained the importance of navigational rights under international law.
Beijing again objected in 2021 as the UK increased its naval presence in the Indo-Pacific, accusing Britain of deploying its Carrier Strike Group to the South China Sea to “flex its naval muscles”. More recently, in July 2026, the Chinese Embassy in London strongly condemned the UK for joining an international statement supporting the 2016 South China Sea arbitration award and urged Britain to stop what it described as “stirring up trouble” in the region.
HMS Tamar has also recently conducted a freedom-of-navigation activity in the South China Sea. In a parliamentary answer published on 8 September, the Ministry of Defence confirmed that the patrol ship operated alongside the Royal Australian Navy on 1 September as part of the UK’s stated commitment to freedom of navigation and overflight under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.
The Royal Navy says HMS Spey and HMS Tamar have themselves conducted freedom-of-navigation missions in disputed waters during their five-year deployment to the Indo-Pacific, sometimes operating independently and sometimes alongside regional partners.
Before Bersama Lima moves into its main operational phase, personnel from the five participating nations will spend time familiarising themselves with different vessels, equipment, procedures and terminology, while senior officers carry out planning for the live exercise.
According to a Royal Navy news update, Lieutenant Commander Cheryl Goodwin, HMS Tamar’s Executive Officer, said: “We’re looking forward to being a part of Bersama Lima 26 – an exercise which unites some of our closest allies, tests the crew in a traditional war-fighting role, and demonstrates the UK’s resolve to maintain stability in the Indo-Pacific region through supporting our partners.”
HMS Tamar is also carrying a Royal New Zealand Navy boarding team during the exercise, adding another element of direct integration between the participating forces.
Lieutenant Williams, a Royal New Zealand Navy officer embarked aboard Tamar, said: “It’s a first for me and my team, but it’s a well-trodden path which has been established through a deep history of our navies working together.”
He added: “We’ve got a lot of experience to share, are always looking to improve and we’re ready to go.”
The Five Power Defence Arrangements were established in 1971 and provide a framework for defence cooperation between the five member states. Regular exercises bring together naval, land and air forces, particularly around Malaysia and Singapore, to practise combined operations and develop common procedures. Both British patrol ships have been forward deployed to the Indo-Pacific since 2021. Their mission, known as Operation Highwall, has included multinational exercises, maritime security operations, sanctions enforcement, humanitarian assistance, defence engagement and freedom-of-navigation activity.
Bersama Lima marks a return to operations for HMS Spey after the vessel spent the summer undergoing maintenance in Singapore. HMS Tamar has remained active across the region, including participation in the US-led Pacific Partnership humanitarian exercise and a visit to Cambodia before its September activity with the Royal Australian Navy in the South China Sea.
The ships passed five years continuously deployed to the Indo-Pacific in September, making them the first Royal Navy vessels to maintain a persistent presence in the region since the handover of Hong Kong in 1997.
During Bersama Lima, Spey and Tamar will operate as part of a larger multinational force, with the live phase testing the five FPDA nations across areas including maritime interdiction, anti-submarine warfare and air defence in and around the South China Sea.

articles.title: Japan’s counterstrike missile goes on public display
articles.body:
- Japan showed its Type 25 surface-to-ship missile launcher to local residents at Camp Kengun in Kumamoto on Oct. 3, the first public showing since deployment.
- The upgraded Type 12 missile has a reported range of about 1,000 km and is Japan's first weapon for its counterstrike capability.
Japan has put its longest-range missile system on public display for the first time since deployment, showing the Type 25 surface-to-ship guided missile launcher to local residents at the Japan Ground Self-Defense Force’s Camp Kengun in Kumamoto on Oct. 3.
Four vehicles, including the missile launcher and an ammunition carrier, were lined up inside the camp’s maintenance facility, Kyodo News reported. A company commander from the 5th Surface-to-Ship Missile Regiment, the unit that operates the system, briefed visitors on the equipment. About 80 people attended the morning session, taking photos and asking soldiers questions.
Photos from the event show the launcher, a heavy multi-axle truck, with its box-shaped launch canisters raised at an angle inside a hangar lined with shipping containers. The display was open to residents of Kumamoto city and people from elsewhere in Kumamoto Prefecture who work or study in the city, with participants applying in advance.
The Type 25 is an upgraded, ground-launched version of Japan’s Type 12 anti-ship missile, built by Mitsubishi Heavy Industries. The original Type 12 has a range of about 200 km (125 miles). The new version can fly about 1,000 km (620 miles), Japanese media report, putting much of the East China Sea, parts of China’s coast and the Korean Peninsula within reach from Kyushu.
It is the first missile Japan has fielded to carry out what the government calls “counterstrike capability,” the ability to hit enemy bases and launch sites, which Tokyo adopted in its 2022 National Security Strategy. Japan’s Defense Ministry describes it as a stand-off weapon, meaning it can strike an invading force from beyond the range of that force’s own weapons.
The missile was deployed to Camp Kengun on March 31, the same day the ministry formally named it the Type 25 surface-to-ship guided missile, or 25SSM. Before that deployment, the Defense Ministry showed the launcher only to a limited group that included Kumamoto Gov. Takashi Kimura, Kumamoto Mayor Kazufumi Onishi and heads of local community councils. Residents had called for a showing open to the general public, Kyodo reported.
Camp Kengun sits in a residential area in the eastern part of Kumamoto city, on Japan’s southwestern island of Kyushu, the closest of Japan’s main islands to the East China Sea and Taiwan.
The Type 25 surface-to-ship missile is one of two new long-range weapons Japan deployed this year. On the same day, the Japan Ground Self-Defense Force sent the Type 25 Hyper Velocity Gliding Projectile, a ballistic weapon with a gliding warhead, to Camp Fuji in Shizuoka Prefecture.
The Defense Ministry plans to add ship-launched and air-launched versions of the Type 25 missile on Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force destroyers and Japan Air Self-Defense Force fighters in fiscal 2027.

articles.title: US to send additional forces to Israel for potential escalation as both countries elections near
articles.body:
The US military has been conducting routine troop rotations in recent weeks, and additional troops and aircraft are expected to arrive in the coming weeks as part of preparations for an escalation in the Middle East, security sources told Walla on Sunday.
Some 3,000 US troops are currently stationed across Israel. Their duties include operating air defense systems, serving as pilots and support crews, and handling logistics and headquarters operations.
The Jerusalem Post previously reported that the Trump administration decided to deploy a third aircraft carrier to the Middle East, along with a second Marine division ahead of the US midterm elections.
The USS Theodore Roosevelt and an additional division of US Marines are currently en route to the Middle East for an extended deployment. The Roosevelt departed from San Francisco last Sunday.
A day later, the USS Makin Island amphibious ready group also departed San Diego, carrying the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit. The force includes about 2,200 Marines and personnel in the expeditionary unit, along with about 2,000 sailors aboard the group's three ships.
Israel's enemies watching Israeli, US elections
A senior Israeli defense official told Walla that Israel’s enemies are watching the elections in Israel and the US and considering whether and how to influence them through terrorist attacks. Such attacks would aim to unsettle the countries’ political systems without triggering a broader escalation.
“They understand that the Israeli response this time will be very aggressive.”
Iran is assessing whether the US is prepared to launch a military campaign against it and is conducting negotiations accordingly. Meanwhile, conditions in Iran are deteriorating on several fronts, particularly the economy. This comes as the US has succeeded in imposing conditions under which oil tankers are departing at nearly prewar levels.
Saudi Arabia, UAE ties to confront Houthis to have larger regional consequences
IDF officials say the campaign against the Houthis presents an opportunity to advance regional initiatives. Much depends on Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates strengthening ties and reaching agreements to confront their shared enemy, the Houthis.
According to senior IDF officials, such cooperation could encourage investment in Lebanon to displace Iranian investment and influence exercised through Hezbollah. It could also help build an anti-Iranian coalition in preparation for another military campaign.
A senior security official told Walla that there is an understanding that anyone who does not join the campaign against the Houthis now will be left alone and “will take hits from them accordingly.”
Preparing for another confrontation with Iran
The IDF is preparing for hostilities with Iran to erupt and escalate rapidly as Tehran struggles to cope with US sanctions and mounting economic pressure.
The military’s main focus is on the operations it would need to carry out if forced to launch extensive strikes against Iran, including identifying targets that would affect the extremist regime in Tehran.
Meanwhile, the IDF continues to coordinate closely with US Central Command, which oversees American military operations in the Middle East, in case Iran attempts to launch surprise missile barrages against Jordan and Israel.
Amichai Stein and Idan Kweller contributed to this report.

articles.title: Russia strikes Kyiv bridge as German chancellor visits Ukraine in show of support
articles.body:
Russia has struck another major bridge in Kyiv as the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, arrived in the capital in a show of support for Ukraine.
A Russian drone hit Kyiv’s key Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River, marking the fourth consecutive day that Russia has targeted bridges used by tens of thousands of residents commuting between the city’s two banks. Video footage showed cars driving across the bridge as the drone plunged into the roadway and exploded in a burst of fire. Two people were injured in the strike, said Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko.
The attack came shortly after Merz arrived in the city on an unannounced visit intended to underline Germany’s backing of Ukraine, as the country enters one of the most precarious periods since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
Germany has become Ukraine’s biggest provider of military aid since Merz entered office in May 2025, surpassing the US as American support has declined.
Kyiv has come under near-constant attack from Russia’s new jet-powered drones in recent weeks, as an intensifying strike campaign increasingly disrupts everyday life in the capital and threatens to leave the city without power this winter.
On his visit, Merz announced that Germany would fund the joint production of drones designed to intercept Russia’s jet-powered drones, adding that “significant technical breakthroughs” in recent weeks were speeding up production.
“This will quickly and tangibly strengthen Ukraine’s air defence,” he said. “And this strengthening is urgently needed.”
The German leader got a taste of the new reality of daily life in the Ukrainian capital. Air-raid sirens sounded repeatedly during his visit, including as Volodymyr Zelenskyy showed him the badly damaged National Academy of Sciences building, where a Russian drone strike killed two people last week.
The Ukrainian president told Merz that people in Kyiv were suffering “terrible nights and days” from the relentless attacks, and called Ukraine’s Russian adversaries “absolute barbarians”.
“We can see the entire pointlessness of this war at this place,” said Merz, adding as he arrived that Ukraine “needs all our support in the coming weeks”. “If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us,” he said.
Russia had already damaged Kyiv’s Northern Bridge and repeatedly struck its Southern Bridge. Although the crossings remain standing, repeated attacks and the threat of further strikes have prompted the city’s authorities to restrict or suspend traffic on five of the city’s six road bridges over the Dnipro, causing temporary closures and large traffic jams.
If Moscow succeeds in seriously damaging Kyiv’s bridges, it could create a logistical nightmare for the city of 3 million people, whose crossings over the Dnipro were last destroyed on a large scale as Nazi German forces retreated in 1943. More than a third of residents live on the left bank while much of the city’s employment and infrastructure is concentrated on the right.
The attacks form part of a broader Russian campaign against civilian and industrial infrastructure inside Ukraine. In recent weeks, strikes have hit logistics hubs, railway lines, datacentres, medical storage facilities and steel plants, alongside a sustained assault on the country’s energy system that is expected to intensify over the winter.
“He [Putin] is counting on constant escalation. He wants this very much,” Zelenskyy said at a press conference alongside Merz. “This is an answer to everyone – to those who believe that all you have to do is simply ask Putin and he will end the war for real. It won’t happen, simply.”
Russia’s foreign ministry on Saturday warned foreign nationals and diplomatic staff against remaining in or travelling to Ukraine. “Responsibility for any possible adverse consequences lies entirely with those who choose to disregard this warning,” the ministry said.
A number of foreign ambassadors, including Germany’s, responded on social media that they intended to remain in Kyiv.
“The EU delegation is staying,” the European Union ambassador, Katarína Mathernová, wrote on X on Sunday. “Threatening us will not stop Europe’s support for Ukraine. It only reminds us why that support matters.”
In Moscow, some pro-war commenters noted with glee that the Russian strikes had continued despite Merz’s arrival. “Russia used to pause strikes on Kyiv during visits by European politicians. Not any more,” wrote Sergei Markov, a prominent pro-war commentator.
The trip is Merz’s second to Ukraine since becoming chancellor. He has been among Kyiv’s most outspoken supporters in Europe and a leading voice warning about Russia’s hybrid campaign against other nations.
Last month, Germany formally accused Moscow of being behind a suspected plot targeting Leipzig/Halle airport, a key logistics hub for western military aid to Ukraine. But Merz is also facing growing discontent at home over his support for Ukraine, as his approval ratings fall.
Germany’s far left and far right are sceptical of support for Ukraine and want Berlin to scale back aid. The pressure has intensified as the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has made big electoral gains.
Alice Weidel, the AfD’s co-leader, wrote in a social media post: “Merz is travelling to Ukraine on Germany’s national holiday and promising further billions in German taxpayer money that is missing from the pension and health insurance funds, while Germany is mired in its worst energy crisis.”

articles.title: EU Rejects Russian Threats to Envoys, Vows Unbroken Kyiv Presence
articles.body:
The EU will not scale back its support for Ukraine or alter the operations of its diplomatic presence in Kyiv in response to Russian warnings directed at foreign missions, European Commission spokesperson Christian Wigand confirmed.
According to RBC-Ukraine and European Pravda, Wigand stated that the EU delegation to Ukraine continues to operate without changes in the capital, dismissing Moscow’s threats as an unsuccessful attempt to intimidate European governments and weaken Western backing for Kyiv.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“This is not the first time Russia has issued such threats. It shows that the Kremlin is losing the war and losing self-control,” Wigand said.
“The European Union will continue to support Ukraine, expose Russia’s irresponsible and dangerous actions, and steadily increase pressure on Moscow.”
The European Commission’s rebuff followed an official dispatch issued on Saturday, Oct. 3, by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Russia, which warned foreign citizens and accredited diplomats in Kyiv of “mortal danger” and pledged to sustain mass aerial bombardments across the capital.
Defense procurement tranches and air defense transfers
Wigand underscored that rather than retreating under Kremlin pressure, European institutions are accelerating military and financial assistance programs to reinforce Ukrainian resilience ahead of the winter heating season.
According to Council of the EU dispatches, member states have approved defense procurement plans totaling €28.3 billion ($31.9 billion) for Ukraine under the multi-year Ukraine Support Loan facility.
Operation Vivaldi Liberates up to 140 Sq Km in Donbas
Concurrently, European capitals have approved the allocation of €6.6 billion ($7.5 billion) through the European Peace Facility (EPF) to reimburse member states for bilateral military assistance delivered to Ukrainian forces.
Strengthening Ukraine’s air and missile defense architecture remains the primary operational priority for European defense coordinators.
To bridge delivery timelines while defense manufacturers scale up serial assembly lines, the EU is evaluating mechanisms to transfer surface-to-air interceptors directly from European national military stockpiles to Ukraine, with inventories to be replenished subsequently using funds allocated under the Ukraine Support Loan.
In addition to defense financing, Brussels is finalizing what officials describe as the most extensive sanctions package against Russia to date.
The diplomatic move follows the EU’s enactment on Sept. 28 of targeted restrictive measures penalizing individuals and entities involved in the unlawful transfer and deportation of Ukrainian children.
Unbroken diplomatic presence
Earlier, The Guardian reported that senior Western diplomats had drafted contingency blueprints to relocate personnel to the western city of Lviv or eastern Poland if Russian strikes deliberately targeted diplomatic representations.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine quickly dismissed claims of an impending withdrawal. Ukrainian MFA spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi confirmed on Friday that no foreign diplomatic missions had submitted relocation notices, emphasizing that established international protocols mandate prior formal notification before any mission moves.
The diplomatic exchanges unfold against an intensifying Russian aerial campaign aimed at degrading municipal utilities, transit infrastructure, and life-support networks across Kyiv.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko warned on Friday that sustaining basic municipal operations under continuous missile and drone barrages has become an urgent matter of “safety and survival,” following consecutive drone strikes that damaged the Southern and Northern bridges spanning the Dnipro River.

articles.title: Brazilians head to polls in pivotal election
articles.body:
Polls close in Brazil’s pivotal election
Polls have closed in Brazil’s hotly contested presidential election, which could reshape the country’s domestic and foreign policy.
The race is dominated by incumbent left-wing President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and his right-wing challenger, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, son of former President Jair Bolsonaro. Lula is seeking a fourth nonconsecutive term in office. More than a dozen other candidates are also on the ballot.
Polls released on the eve of the election showed Lula and Bolsonaro neck and neck. Quaest put them at 46% and 45%, respectively, while Datafolha had Lula at 45% and Bolsonaro at 42%, with both surveys showing a statistical tie. If neither candidate wins more than half of votes, a runoff will be held on October 25. All other candidates are polling in the low single digits, but their endorsements could prove important in a second round.
Brazilians will also elect all 513 federal congress members, 54 of the country’s 81 senators, 27 governors and some regional legislatures.
Lula campaigned on his left-leaning Workers’ Party platform, promising continued welfare programs, state-funded development and income redistribution. He has framed the vote as a choice between “strengthening democracy and barbarism.”
Bolsonaro called for “change,” blaming Lula’s policies for high living costs and promising tougher security policies and tax cuts. The 45-year-old senator for Rio de Janeiro has also leaned heavily on the image of his father, known to supporters as “mito” – “the legend.”
Jair Bolsonaro, 71, was sentenced to 27 years behind bars over attempting to overturn the results of the 2022 presidential election, which he lost to Lula. He has denied wrongdoing. He spent several months in prison after breaking house arrest monitoring rules before being hospitalized in March 2026 over health issues and eventually transferred back to “temporary” house arrest that has since been extended.
Why does this vote matter?
Brazil is a founding member of BRICS and has played a prominent role in the group. Under Lula, Brasilia has pursued a policy focused on strengthening multipolarity and resisting Western pressure, particularly from Washington.
The Trump administration has placed renewed emphasis on US dominance in the Western Hemisphere under what it calls the “Donroe Doctrine,” a modern reinterpretation of the 19th-century hegemonic political strategy known as the Monroe Doctrine.
Washington has said it intends to strengthen US influence across the Americas while preventing rival powers, particularly China, from gaining strategic footholds there.
Opposing ‘colonization’
During his current term, Lula has repeatedly criticized the US over what he described as attempts to undermine multipolarity and impose its will on other nations.
Last year, India and Brazil stepped up talks on trade and investment after both countries were hit with 50% tariffs by the US. Lula also called for a coordinated BRICS response to Washington’s tariff policies, accusing Trump of attempts to “dismantle multilateralism” and promote “unilateralism, where he negotiates one-on-one with other countries.”
The Brazilian president also sharply condemned the US kidnapping of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in early 2026. In March, he proposed boosting defense cooperation with South Africa to reduce reliance on foreign weapons, arguing that both nations could be vulnerable to “invasion.”
In late September, he openly accused Trump of seeking to “colonize” Brazil and gain control of its natural resources. “What Trump wants is to colonize Brazil, to take our wealth, steal our future and leave us behind,” he stated at the time.
‘Trump’s candidate’?
Flavio Bolsonaro, whom Lula has described as “Trump’s candidate,” has emphasized his affinity with the US president and repeatedly praised him, while denying receiving assistance from Washington for his campaign. He has insisted that Brazil should seek better deals with the US, including on rare earth minerals – a topic that has been repeatedly invoked by US President Donald Trump in his talks with various nations, including Ukraine and Russia.
The senator also promised a “flood of investments” from the US if he wins. “Brazil and the United States will once again have a high-level and long-term relationship, including the largest trade and investment agreement in our history!” Bolsonaro wrote in a post on X in June.
He has also vowed to “truly combat Brazilian terrorist organizations and restore sovereignty to more than 50 million Brazilians who live in areas dominated by them,” without specifying which groups he meant.
Bolsonaro has also reportedly pledged to join the US campaign against drug cartels. The American military has at times targeted boats supposedly belonging to traffickers, killing dozens of people.
Shadow of interference
Brazilian authorities have opened a probe into allegations that the US government funded activities aimed at interfering in the election and undermining the legitimacy of the country’s Supreme Federal Court, Agencia Brasil reported on Friday.
That followed a report by the Guardian earlier in the week, claiming that the White House had planned to allocate $1 million for a project titled “Countering Lawfare and Censorship in Brazil.”
US social media giant Meta also blocked the advertising account on Facebook used by Lula’s campaign, preventing it from running new ads just days before the first round. The account was restored later the same day, with Meta providing no immediate explanation.
In September, Lula cited a confidential assessment by the Brazilian Intelligence Agency, which warned that a risk of US interference in the vote was allegedly at a “critical level.”
Trump avoided openly endorsing any candidates ahead of the elections but stated he was following the vote “very closely.”
“Brazil is a very important country. The people of Brazil are fantastic. These are very important elections,” he said on Thursday.
Moscow has expressed its hope that the Sunday vote would be held “without any adverse external interference.” “We are open to… continuing our cooperation with our Brazilian partners across the entire agenda,” the head of the Russian Foreign Ministry’s Latin American Department, Aleksandr Shetinin, told TASS.

articles.title: Yemeni presidency announces offensive to retake Houthi territory
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Yemeni presidency announces offensive to retake all Houthi territory
Yemen's leader announced on Sunday the start of a new military operation to retake all territory held by the Houthis, even as the group made fresh gains on the ground, effectively encircling a government-held city.
The announcement sets an ambitious goal for the embattled government, which recently lost large swathes of the country's Red Sea coastline and areas around the Bab al-Mandab Strait - a chokepoint for international shipping - after a lightning offensive by the Iran-backed Houthis.
Yemen's government has struggled to roll back the surge, even with the military support of Saudi Arabia, where the Houthis said they had attacked oil infrastructure in the capital yet again on Sunday.
"I announce today the start of military operations to retake the remaining territories of the republic and extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory," Rashad al-Alimi, the head of Yemen's presidential council, said in a statement.
Alimi called on all the armed forces "to begin carrying out their assigned missions, in accordance with the approved plans, until the country is liberated from the grip of the Houthi terrorist militia".
The statement came just hours after the Houthis cut a vital supply route linking the besieged city of Taiz with the government's interim capital Aden, according to four security sources.
The Houthi advance followed days of heavy fighting in and around the city.
"We were informed that the Houthis had taken control of the al-Safiya area, where they cut the main road and took control of the police station," a police source in the area told AFP.
Three sources with the Yemeni military also confirmed Houthi control over the area and the supply route, with traffic along the road halted and the group now surrounding Taiz city.
The military sources added that fighting in the area was ongoing.
Taiz itself remains under the control of government forces but has long been besieged from the north, east and west by Houthi fighters and remains one of the main fronts in Yemen's long-running civil war.
"They've achieved the military objective of isolating Taiz from Aden, even if they haven't fully taken control of it," Farea Al-Muslimi, research fellow at the Chatham House think-tank, told AFP.
Muslimi also downplayed expectations over what the coming government offensive might accomplish.
"In my opinion, it's meaningless, he added.
Saudi attacks
Following several years of relative calm, Yemen's civil war reignited in July against the backdrop of the wider conflict in the Middle East.
It has also drawn in Saudi Arabia - leader of an anti-Houthi military coalition since 2015 - with the group regularly claiming attacks on the kingdom's territory in recent weeks and declaring a blockade of its ships in the Red Sea.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree on Sunday said the group launched ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi energy giant Aramco's sites in Riyadh and in the oil-rich Khurais area in the east.
"The strikes were precise, causing large fires at the targeted sites," Saree said on X.
Saudi oil exports were already under pressure thanks to Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
The Houthi's Al-Masirah TV channel reported Saudi strikes Sunday in the northern governorates of al-Jawf and Saada, saying at least two people had been wounded.
They came a day after Yemen's government said its forces struck Houthi targets around the country, including in the capital Sanaa, the northwestern governorate of Saada and the group's positions near Taiz in the southwest.
The Yemeni government's air capabilities, however, are limited, and the Saudi-led coalition has long been the primary force carrying out airstrikes against the Houthis.
Experts believe the recent operations have most likely been conducted by Saudi warplanes as well.
Yemen is one of the poorest countries in the world and remains gripped by a vast humanitarian crisis that has unspooled since the civil war broke out in 2014.
That year the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa from the Saudi-backed government, before going on to take control of much of the country's north, with Riyadh's international coalition intervening the following year.

Zelenskyy surprised by Russia's "savage desire" to escalate war, says it was Russia that struck first
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has expressed surprise at Russia's "savage desire" to escalate the war daily and stressed that Russia was the first to launch strikes, including against warehouses belonging to Ukrainian postal services Nova Poshta and Ukrposhta.

Now they are striking bridges. Do they really think we won't respond? They are striking data centres. All of this affects people. This is certainly not some kind of military infrastructure. Details: Zelenskyy noted that he is "surprised by this savage desire to escalate every single day."

articles.title: Russia Launched 1,900 Drones and 25 Missiles This Week, Zelensky Says
articles.body:
Russian forces launched more than 1,900 strike drones, 1,700 guided aerial bombs, and 25 missiles of various types against Ukraine over the past week, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Sunday, Oct. 4.
Writing on Telegram, he reported that over 800 of the unmanned aerial vehicles deployed in the weekly barrage were high-speed, turbojet-powered variants, which travel at higher velocities and altitudes that complicate interception by ground-based mobile air defense units.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The weekly tally followed an overnight bombardment into Sunday morning during which Russian forces launched 135 strike drones across Ukrainian territory, including more than 50 jet-powered models.
Incoming munitions targeted regions including Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Kharkiv, Donetsk, Sumy, and Zaporizhzhia, damaging residential buildings, utility networks, and municipal life-support systems, triggering localized power outages across several communities.
Zelensky confirmed that overnight drone strikes in the northern city of Sumy struck a commercial pharmaceutical storage depot, killing one person. In Dnipro, a Russian strike hit a communications enterprise, injuring at least six people, while a follow-on drone hit the North Bridge in Kyiv.
“It is vital that Ukraine does not stand alone against this terror,” Zelensky stated, emphasizing that international partners must respond to Moscow’s expanding reliance on turbojet loitering munitions.
UN: Ukraine Civilian Casualties Surge 55% in 2026
Capital bridge strikes and transit disruption
The Sunday morning strike on Kyiv’s North Bridge marks the second consecutive aerial attack targeting the strategic river crossing within a 24-hour window, compounding logistical strain across the capital.
Emergency services and municipal transit engineers were dispatched to the bridge after incoming fire blasted a detonation crater into the road deck. Municipal authorities are assessing the physical destruction to determine whether vehicular crossings between the eastern and western districts of the city must face further transit restrictions.
The follow-up attack follows a direct hit on the morning of Saturday, when a Russian turbojet loitering munition struck the North Bridge, tearing up road surface asphalt and severing overhead electrical contact cables that power municipal trolleybuses. 
Klitschko confirmed that two civilians sustained injuries in Saturday’s bridge strike, with one victim treated at the scene and a second hospitalized.
The consecutive hits on the North Bridge follow the complete closure of the South Bridge to vehicular traffic on Friday after repeated drone impacts damaged roadway sections, bridge piers, and structural barriers shielding the Green Line metro crossing.
Сounter-drone interceptors
The surge in weekly bombardments coincides with high-level bilateral defense consultations in the capital following the unannounced arrival in Kyiv of German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Leading a government and industrial delegation that includes German Minister for Economic Affairs Katharina Reiche and 10 defense and energy corporate executives, Merz arrived on Sunday to formally guarantee expedited military deliveries, including 1,000 newly developed interceptor systems designed specifically to defeat high-speed, turbojet-powered Shahed drones.
Welcoming the German chancellor’s visit, Zelensky commended Berlin’s consistent defense leadership and confirmed that bilateral teams are preparing joint defense agreements to bolster Ukraine’s and Europe’s layered air defense architectures.
“Germany consistently demonstrates leadership in protecting the lives of Ukrainians from Russian strikes,” Zelensky said. “Today we are preparing decisions so that we in Ukraine and throughout Europe have more opportunities to defend ourselves. There will be important agreements between Ukraine and Germany.”

articles.title: American bomber fleet departs Britain
articles.body:
All US bombers deployed to RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire have returned to their home stations in the United States, ending the latest sustained deployment of American heavy bombers at the British airbase, according to US European Command.
European Command confirmed on 4 October that the aircraft “are redeploying to their home stations”, while a US Department of Defense official separately confirmed that every American bomber deployed to Fairford had now left the base.
“While operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real-time, we can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have redeployed to their home stations in the United States,” a US Air Force statement said.
The aircraft remaining at Fairford before the departure were B-1B Lancer bombers. The New York Times, citing two US officials, reported that 12 B-1s were involved in the redeployment and that at least three had reached South Dakota by Sunday. No reason for the withdrawal has been given publicly by the Pentagon or US European Command.
European Command said American bombers routinely deploy internationally as part of global readiness and operational requirements, without providing further detail on the decision to bring the Fairford aircraft home. “US Air Force bombers routinely operate around the world to support global force readiness and operational requirements,” the US statement said.
The service added that its bomber force remained capable of carrying out long-range operations directly from the continental United States. “The Airmen that operate America’s bomber force, including B-1s, B-2s, and B-52s, remain ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities – including through operations that launch and recover from the continental United States – anywhere, anytime.”
RAF Fairford is a Royal Air Force station used extensively by the United States Air Force and serves as a forward operating location for US strategic bomber deployments to Europe. Its long runway and supporting infrastructure allow aircraft including the B-1B Lancer, B-2 Spirit and B-52 Stratofortress to operate from the Gloucestershire base.
The airfield has hosted a substantial US bomber presence during 2026. B-1 and B-52 aircraft operated from Fairford during American military operations connected with the war with Iran, making the base one of the principal European locations supporting the deployment of US long-range strike aircraft.
Six B-52 Stratofortress bombers had already departed Fairford earlier in the year, leaving B-1 Lancers as the remaining deployed bomber force at the base by the beginning of October.
The B-1B is a supersonic long-range conventional bomber operated by the US Air Force. Although originally developed during the Cold War with a nuclear role, the aircraft was subsequently converted to a conventional-only mission and has been used extensively for long-range strike operations.

articles.title: Russia has reduced use of ballistic missiles ahead of winter – Dutch analyst
articles.body:
Russia has reduced use of ballistic missiles ahead of winter – Dutch analyst
He expressed this opinion in an exclusive comment to Ukrinform. Bolder is a strategic analyst and defense expert at the Hague Center for Strategic Studies (HCSS) and a former lieutenant colonel in the Royal Netherlands Air Force.
Bolder said that Russia was currently escalating its attacks on Ukrainian territory and that these attacks were having a severe impact on the lives of ordinary Ukrainian civilians. He said this was horrific. According to the analyst, the main weapons Russia was currently using were the Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered drones. Ukraine did not yet have a complete response to these drones, although it was making very active efforts to destroy them as well. The effectiveness of intercepting them was gradually increasing and had already exceeded 50%.
At the same time, Bolder noted that the number of ballistic missiles Russia was using was currently lower than before. In his view, this suggested that, as Ukraine did not yet have a real response to the jet-powered drones, Russia was refraining from using ballistic missiles and was likely saving them for further use during the winter.
He also drew attention to the development of Ukrainian ballistic missile capabilities. In his view, the creation of such systems could have a dual significance: in addition to providing Ukraine with the ability to strike Russian launchers, it would give the country a technological foundation for developing its own interceptor missiles.
At the same time, he identified the need to scale up production of such systems to sufficient volumes as the key challenge.
The analyst also warned of possible problems for Ukraine in winter. He said these could affect not only electricity supplies, as the country had a significant number of generators, but also the operation of water treatment and sewage systems, as well as electricity supplies to defense industry enterprises.
In his assessment, the intensification of strikes on civilian infrastructure could be linked to the situation on the battlefield, where Russian forces, he said, were suffering significant losses and had recently lost some territory.
Bolder said that a serious problem was that businesses were being left without electricity. He said that, in effect, Russia wanted to suffocate Ukraine and make the Ukrainian economic model unviable for a very long time so that Ukraine would eventually become exhausted. At the same time, he said, efforts were also being made to persuade Europe to stop supporting Ukraine, leaving it with no choice but to accept Putin's demands. However, he noted that history showed this never worked that way: the more strongly one state attacked a people or another country, the more people rallied around their flag.

articles.title: Israel blows up schools, flattens villages in southern Lebanon
articles.body:
Israel blows up schools, flattens villages in southern Lebanon
TEHRAN — Israeli forces escalated their campaign of artillery shelling, airstrikes, and controlled demolitions across southern Lebanon over the weekend, turning border villages into uninhabitable wreckage while Washington provides political cover for the ongoing aggression.
Explosives in schools and destruction of border villages
According to local media outlets, the latest wave of destruction hit hardest in the Marjayoun and Tyre districts. In Houla, Israeli soldiers rigged a private school building with heavy explosives before blowing it up and setting fire to nearby homes.
Similar demolitions shook Al-Mansouri, where massive detonations sent clouds of white smoke rising above residential neighborhoods, rattling windows as far away as Tyre. The town’s public school had already been mostly destroyed during earlier raids.
Lebanese news outlets also reported relentless artillery bombardment across Wadi Al-Hujeir, Nabatieh Al-Fawqa, Kfarromman, and Baraachit. Israeli warplanes launched strikes on Kfar Tebnit, Bani Hayyan, and the outskirts of Mayfadoun and Zawtar al-Sharqiyah, while low-flying fighter jets buzzed towns across the south.
According to local reports, Israeli troops currently occupy more than 60 southern communities, carrying out systematic demolitions to ensure civilian populations cannot return.
The American shield and occupation costs
This campaign continues despite the “Framework Agreement” signed in Washington on June 26. Advertised by American officials as a step toward Israeli withdrawal and Lebanese army deployment, the deal has produced no pullback.
Instead, Tel Aviv has used the agreement to entrench its presence while demanding unilateral Lebanese concessions.
The ongoing occupation poses severe daily hazards for local populations trying to check their land. On September 30, a Lebanese army serviceman was severely injured alongside three civilians near Nabatieh al-Fawqa when a leftover explosive charge detonated during a property inspection escort.
Israeli forces are not operating without cost. An Israeli military spokesperson confirmed Sunday that an officer was moderately injured and a soldier seriously hurt in an operational explosion in southern Lebanon on Friday.
Meanwhile, figures cited from Israel’s war ministry show that 1,318 Israeli military and security personnel have died across all battlefronts since October 2023.

articles.title: German chancellor in Kyiv calls on Putin to "stop this senseless war"

Merz said that while Ukraine is preparing for winter, its infrastructure is being attacked every day.
"I appeal once again to the Russian leadership, to the Russian president: Stop this war! We can talk, but only when the weapons fall silent – and the weapons must fall silent," he said. [N.B. Ukrainska Pravda does not recognise Putin as president – ed.]

articles.title: Ukraine to Close Its Current Budget Deficit by Year’s End
articles.body:
Ukraine will eliminate its wartime budget deficit before the end of the year, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced in an interview with Reuters.
Zelensky stated that negotiations conducted by Ukrainian officials in Brussels had produced a viable framework to manage the state’s short-term financing gap while maintaining steady procurement for the armed forces.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Over the past several months we worked on our financial deficit. We will close the current deficit by the end of the year,” Zelensky said in comments released by the presidential administration. “We still have some issues to work through, but we will close the deficit.”
The president described resolving the shortfall as a major success for Ukraine, his negotiating team, and European partners, emphasizing that stabilization of the state budget was achieved through joint fiscal adjustments and credit mechanisms.
Frontloading EU loans and 2027 drone contracts
Zelensky explained that the government intends to advance portions of European credit allocations originally scheduled for 2027 into early January, ensuring that domestic defense contractors receive early capital allocations to maintain uninterrupted production lines.
“It was not easy. We worked with our budget, with our partners, especially the European Union, and we will also try to partially use loan funds for next year,” Zelensky said. “We will bring this closer to January and use this money to order drones for January and February 2027. My team returned from Brussels and reported. Everything is working well. I hope that this will continue.”
Vilnius Airport Closes as NATO Jets Scramble Over Suspected Drone
The drive to secure early procurement funding follows discussions between Ukrainian economic officials and European counterparts in Brussels, where Ukrainian Finance Minister Serhiy Marchenko outlined long-term financing requirements for the coming fiscal year.
Marchenko previously cautioned that Ukraine could face a prospective financial shortfall of approximately €69 billion ($78 billion) in 2027, projecting requirements of roughly €40 billion ($45 billion) for defense operations and €29 billion ($33 billion) to maintain civilian state administration and public services.
Reform conditionality and frozen asset discussions
The planned deployment of credit lines unfolds as Brussels manages disbursements under the EU’s €90 billion ($102 billion) support loan facility covering the 2026-2027 period.
Under the framework’s 2026 allocation of €45 billion ($51 billion), the European Commission has disbursed approximately €15 billion ($17 billion). European officials have emphasized that subsequent payment tranches remain linked to verified reform benchmarks, focusing on anti-corruption enforcement, judicial governance, and public administration transparency.
European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos noted during donor coordination sessions that completing statutory reforms remains the primary mechanism for unlocking committed funding pipelines, urging Ukrainian institutions to coordinate closely to meet technical criteria.
Concurrently, European capitals have debated proposals to utilize immobilized Russian sovereign assets to support Ukraine’s defense and recovery.
While Kyiv has advocated using portions of the roughly €210 billion ($239 billion) in Russian central bank reserves immobilized across Europe – principally held in Belgium through the Euroclear depository – member states including Belgium, France, and Italy have urged caution regarding potential legal liabilities and financial market stability.
To supplement bilateral budgetary aid, European institutions are also integrating Ukraine into wider industrial initiatives. The European Commission approved €325 million ($368.6 million) to fund five European Defence Projects of Common Interest (EDPCI), with Ukraine participating in four collaborative frameworks.
