articles.title: Ukraine's deep strikes have wrecked over half of Russia's oil refining capacity, Defense Ministry says
articles.body:
Ukraine's deep strikes have wrecked over half of Russia's oil refining capacity, Defense Ministry says
Over 51% of Russia's oil refining capacity has been disabled by Ukrainian attacks, the Defense Ministry reported on Oct. 4.
Ukraine has systematically targeted Russia's oil and gas infrastructure in long-range strikes, dramatically increasing its campaign against oil refineries in the past two years. Kyiv considers refineries valid military targets, as they supply both fuel and funds to the Russian armed forces.
Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara reported on the consequences of Ukraine's strategy in an update on Oct. 4. Citing analysts from Ukraine's intelligence services, Defense Ministry, and General Staff, Khmara said that over 51% of Russia's oil refining capacity has been disabled.
"This is the result of carefully planned, systematic, and comprehensive actions aimed at crippling the Russian war machine and destroying its military-economic potential," Khmara said.
"Fifty-one percent of the damaged oil refining capacity is a significant blow to the enemy's economy, to its ability to wage aggression, and to supply its military formations."
The Defense Ministry listed recent attacks at Russia's Moscow, Yaroslavl, Kirishi, Perm, Ilsky, Saratov, and Syzran refineries in its report.
The ministry's assessment marks an increase from the 45% drop in Russian refining capacity reported by Ukraine's General Staff on Sept. 21.
It also follows a decree from Russian President Vladimir Putin, signed Sept. 28, restricting access to data on the country's oil refineries and energy exports amid Ukraine's escalating deep strikes.
Ukraine's long-range strike drones and missiles have proved capable of regularly reaching targets more than 1,500 kilometers (930 miles) from Ukrainian-controlled territory. The military reported a new record on Sept. 9, after a Fire Point FP-1 drone struck a Russian gas facility 3,200 kilometers (1,988 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
The Defense Ministry reported on Oct. 4 that Ukraine tripled its production and procurement of long-range strike drones in 2026 — and that it hopes to keep growing.
"This is not the limit," the ministry said. "We will continue to scale up our long-range strike capabilities."

articles.title: Russia May Be Running Secret Mesh Relays Inside Kyiv to Guide Shahed Strikes
articles.body:

Russia May Be Running Secret Mesh Relays Inside Kyiv to Guide Shahed Strikes
Russian forces may be using a small number of radio relay devices operating inside Kyiv to establish temporary communication links with Shahed-type attack drones and adjust their flight during strikes, according to Ukrainian defense technology adviser Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Beskrestnov said on October 3 that he believes Russian Mesh radio relays are periodically activated in the Ukrainian capital, potentially providing a short-term control channel for incoming drones.
“Right now, I insist that enemy Mesh radio relays are being switched on in Kyiv, providing a temporary short-term control channel for Shaheds to adjust strikes. Not many. Perhaps one to three. Such relays are difficult to find, but they must be searched for,” Beskrestnov said.
According to Beskrestnov, the presence of such devices could complicate efforts to protect Kyiv using electronic warfare systems, as the drones could retain a communication channel during the final stage of an attack.
He pointed to previous Russian strikes in Kyiv, including an attack on a Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) building, as evidence supporting his assessment.
“At the moment of the strike, there were no other Shahed relay drones in the sky. I also analyzed other strikes on Kyiv bridges and the possibility of organizing long-range Mesh channels from Russia at those moments,” he said.
Beskrestnov also raised concerns about Russian access to information on the location of Ukrainian air defense systems deployed around critical infrastructure. Images showing air defense equipment on Kyiv bridges have circulated online, while such deployments are difficult to conceal because tens of thousands of people use the crossings daily, he said.
As long as Russia maintains the ability to control Shahed drones in real time, Beskrestnov said, both infrastructure and air defense systems could potentially be targeted.
He argued that accurately striking individual structural elements of a bridge, such as supports or cables, would require a stable control channel that remains active until the final stage of the drone’s flight.
Beskrestnov stressed that his assessment of Russian relay devices operating inside Kyiv remains a hypothesis. Ukrainian specialists continue examining debris from downed Russian drones for evidence of alternative communication systems.
“Let me be wrong in my opinion about the relays,” Beskrestnov said. “I also want to say that we carefully examine all debris. We do not find any other ‘secret’ means of communication.”
The assessment follows earlier concerns over relay infrastructure outside Ukraine. On September 29, Ukraine’s State Border Guard Service said Belarus periodically activates relay systems that can strengthen communications for Russian drones during attacks on Ukraine.
In June, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called on Belarusian leader Alexander Lukashenko to dismantle relay equipment that Kyiv said was being used to support Russian drone operations.

articles.title: Yemen’s Saudi-backed government launches military drive to retake all Houthi-held territory
articles.body:
Yemen’s Saudi-backed government has announced the start of a new military operation to retake all territory held by the Houthis, even as the militant group made fresh gains on the ground, reportedly encircling a government-held city.
Rashad al-Alimi, the head of Yemen’s presidential council, said in a statement on Sunday: “I announce today the start of military operations to retake the remaining territories of the republic and extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory.”
The announcement sets an ambitious goal for the embattled government, which recently lost swathes of the country’s Red Sea coastline and areas around the Bab al-Mandab strait – a chokepoint for international shipping – after a lightning offensive by the Iran-backed Houthis.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government has struggled to roll back the surge, even with the military support of Saudi Arabia. The Houthis have increasingly targeted Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, and on Sunday said they had attacked oil infrastructure in the capital again.
The statement came just hours after the Houthis cut a vital supply route linking the besieged city of Taiz with the government’s interim capital, Aden, according to four security sources.
The Houthi advance followed days of heavy fighting in and around the city.
“We were informed that the Houthis had taken control of the al-Safiya area, where they cut the main road and took control of the police station,” a police source in the area said.
Three sources with the Yemeni military also confirmed Houthi control over the area and the supply route, with traffic along the road halted and the group now surrounding Taiz city. Fighting in the area was ongoing, they added.
Sources from both sides told AFP on Sunday that fighting in and around the western province of Taiz had killed more than 70 people over the past day.
Sources from the internationally recognised government reported that 34 government troops were killed – 20 on the edge of Taiz province in neighbouring Lahj – while Houthi military sources said 39 of their fighters were killed in fighting across Taiz and in border areas with Lahj.
Taiz city itself remains under the control of government forces but has long been besieged from the north, east and west by Houthi fighters and remains one of the main fronts in Yemen’s long-running civil war.
A Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said on Sunday the group launched ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi energy company Aramco’s sites in Riyadh and in Khurais area in the east, causing large fires.
The attacks were in response to what the Houthis claimed were 50 Saudi-led air and missile strikes in Yemen in the past 12 hours.
There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi Arabia.
Saudi oil exports were already under pressure due to Iran’s blockade of the strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
The Houthi’s Al-Masirah TV channel reported Saudi strikes on Sunday in the northern governorates of al-Jawf and Saada, saying at least two people had been wounded.
With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

articles.title: All B-1 Bombers Leave RAF Fairford in Hasty Departure from UK Base
articles.body:
All 12 American bombers deployed in Britain rapidly returned to the U.S. on Oct. 4 following security concerns about a potential Iranian threat to their base in the U.K.
The dozen B-1B Lancer bombers, which were stationed at RAF Fairford amid ongoing hostilities with Iran, departed over the course of a day, local aircraft spotters said. The U.S. military later confirmed the unexpected departure of the aircraft.
“All U.S. bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have redeployed to their home stations in the United States,” the Pentagon and U.S. European Command said in statements to Air & Space Forces Magazine.
The U.S. military emphasized that bombers could still strike targets across the globe from the continental United States—something B-1B, B-2 Spirit, and B-52 Stratofortress bombers all did during the height of operations against Iran this spring.
“The Airmen that operate America’s bomber force, including B-1s, B-2s, and B-52s, remain ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities—including through operations that launch and recover from the continental United States—anywhere, anytime,” the statement read.
Still, stationing bombers at RAF Fairford sharply reduced the flight time U.S. bombers needed to strike targets in Iran. The open-source group Military Air Tracking Alliance recorded 29 separate bombers that deployed to RAF Fairford, located in southwest England, at different points during the conflict.
The departure of the last 12 bombers comes a week after arrests were made following a suspected plot against the base. Six people have been arrested in connection with the episode. U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were “strong indications” that Iran was behind the threat.
Burnham and his predecessor Keir Starmer allowed the U.S. to use the base to attack Iran for what the U.K. government called self-defense strikes. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said in July it considered RAF Fairford a legitimate target because of the U.S. bombers deployed there.
At the height of the deployment during Operation Epic Fury, the U.S. had around two dozen bombers deployed to RAF Fairford at a single time—some 18 B-1B and half a dozen B-52H bombers. Since the U.S. reached a shaky ceasefire with Iran in April, the bombers have mostly conducted training missions, and the B-52s left months ago. One B-1B that arrived just last week to replace another bomber was part of the exodus on Oct. 4.
RAF Fairford does not have permanent assigned U.S. Air Force aircraft, but the base has a wing dedicated to supporting U.S. operations and is considered the main U.S. bomber site in Europe, having regularly hosted U.S. aircraft for years.
The Air Force permanently stations aircraft in the U.K. at RAF Lakenheath, which hosts F-35A Lightning II and F-15E Strike Eagle fighters that have deployed to the Middle East to operate against Iran. Lakenheath also serves as a stopover for fighters heading to and from the Middle East from the U.S. Nearby, RAF Mildenhall hosts KC-135 tankers that belong to the 100th Air Refueling Wing stationed at the base.
The U.S. has also been rotating its fighters based in the Middle East, sending fresh F-16 Fighting Falcon and F-35s units to the region, primarily from the Air National Guard.

articles.title: Merz Makes Surprise Kyiv Visit, Pledges 1,000 Drone Interceptors
articles.body:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived unannounced in Kyiv on Sunday, Oct. 4, on a high-stakes solidarity visi, Der Spiegel reported.
Arriving in the Ukrainian capital by special train alongside a high-level government and corporate delegation, Merz stated that European security remains inextricably bound to Ukraine’s defense, warning that failing to repel Moscow’s invasion would directly imperil the North Atlantic alliance.

“If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us,” Merz told reporters upon arrival at Kyiv’s central railway station.
The chancellor emphasized that his travel to Kyiv was intended to reaffirm Berlin’s strategic reliability as Russian forces escalate bombardments against critical utilities and transport links across the country.
“Ukraine needs all our support over the coming weeks,” Merz said, observing that despite sustained Russian aerial assaults, Ukrainian society refuses to buckle under military terror. “Today I will tell President [Volodymyr] Zelensky: ‘You can continue to count on our help.’”
According to German government officials cited by Der Spiegel, Merz intends to guarantee the rapid supply of 1,000 newly developed interceptor systems engineered to destroy jet-powered Shahed drones.
The chancellor is accompanied on the mission by German Minister for Economic Affairs Katharina Reiche alongside a 10-member delegation of chief executives and senior industrialists representing Germany’s defense-manufacturing and commercial energy sectors.

Domestic political headwinds
Merz’s unannounced visit follows repeated warnings from Berlin that air defense shortfalls represent the primary threat to Ukraine’s wartime resilience ahead of the heating season.
Speaking in Berlin on Sept. 29, Merz described territorial air defense as Ukraine’s “weakest point,” confirming that the German government has engaged in intensive diplomatic consultations with European partners to assemble emergency military packages ahead of the European Council summit in Brussels on Oct. 15-16.
The chancellor has framed continued military assistance to Kyiv as an imperative for continental stability. During a recent address in Münster, Merz argued that Western strength and unity remain prerequisites for any future peace negotiations with the Kremlin, cautioning that a Russian-dictated peace would destabilize the continent, trigger mass refugee movements, and leave Europe structurally insecure.
The high-profile trip also unfolds against acute domestic political friction within Germany, where populist and pro-Kremlin factions have mobilized voter discontent over economic pressures and military spending.
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) – which opposes arms shipments to Kyiv and demands an immediate resumption of Russian natural gas imports – achieved historic electoral gains in September, capturing roughly 44 percent of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt before securing first place in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
Despite rising electoral polarization, Merz reaffirmed that Germany will not waver in its defense commitments to Ukraine, arguing that protecting Kyiv’s sovereignty remains the baseline foundation for Germany’s own long-term peace and economic prosperity.

A Tu-95MS crashed in Russia, killing 8 military personnel, some of whom may have been involved in missile strikes on Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
A Tu-95MS crashed in Russia’s Far East, killing 8 military personnel. At least three may have been involved in missile strikes on Ukraine.
In Russia’s Amur Oblast, 8 Russian military personnel were killed when a Tu-95MS strategic bomber crashed. At least three of them may have been involved in missile strikes on Ukrainian cities, Russian sources report, UNN writes.
Details
The aircraft crashed on October 1 near the village of Krasnoyarovo. Russia’s Defense Ministry said that the Tu-95MS was carrying out a training flight and crashed in an uninhabited area. Initially, the Russian side reported that 6 crew members had been killed.
However, Mikhail Piven, head of the Mazanovsky District of Amur Oblast, published a photograph of the deceased crew listing 8 military personnel.
Some of those killed may have been involved in strikes on Ukraine
Ukrainian military blogger Anatolii Shtefan, "Shtirlitz," claims that at least three of those killed were directly involved in missile attacks on Ukrainian cities — they handled the methodological support of the strikes and issued and carried out orders to launch cruise missiles. At the same time, he did not name them, so it is currently impossible to independently verify this information.
It is known that Lieutenant Colonel Fyodor Pavlyukov was among those killed — he was deputy commander for flight training of the 182nd Heavy Bomber Aviation Regiment. In 2021–2024, he commanded a Tu-95MS squadron.
Aircraft from this aviation regiment were involved in missile strikes on Ukraine. As early as 2022, Ukrainian intelligence included Pavlyukov on a list of Russian pilots who, according to its data, were being trained to carry out strikes on Ukraine from the territory of Belarus.

articles.title: Iran says Hormuz will not reopen until conditions are met
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran says Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until conditions are met
The Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until seven Iranian conditions set out in a June interim agreement with the US are met, state media reported Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf as saying on Sunday.
Iran presented a proposal during the UN General Assembly under which the Strait of Hormuz waterway could be reopened and normal maritime passage restored within seven days if the conditions were met, with the US replying to this proposal last week via Qatari intermediaries.
"The position of the Islamic Republic of Iran is completely clear and firm, and the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened until our seven conditions, based on the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, are met," Ghalibaf, who is Iran's top negotiator, was quoted as saying.
He said Washington "must understand that the period of dragging out the (diplomatic) process and dictating one-sided demands is over".
Iran says no nuclear discussions
A Foreign Ministry spokesperson said on Sunday that Tehran had clarified its broad positions via mediators to the US response but that additional points remained to be communicated to Washington.
"The Americans' propositions are more or less in line with their previous positions, specifically on the nuclear issue. We told them our focus in this stage is the issue of the Strait of Hormuz and the return to security in this waterway requires clear steps from the US," spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said.
He also denied Tehran had offered UN nuclear watchdog inspections of its nuclear facilities in exchange for US sanctions relief, saying Iran had not entered into nuclear discussions with Washington.
The document being circulated outlines a seven-day period of trust-building aimed at returning the two sides to an enhanced version of the memorandum of understanding agreed in June, including concrete steps on Iran's nuclear programme, an official briefed on the talks said last week.
The disagreement centres on the sequencing of the steps rather than the components of the plan, the official added.
Warning from Araghchi
Qatar has been shuttling messages between Washington and Tehran in an effort to end the conflict and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the conduit for a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas before the war that began at the end of February with US and Israeli attacks on Iran.
The June memorandum of understanding led to a brief ceasefire and included provisions on the strait and Iran's nuclear programme.
Separately, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told foreign ambassadors and diplomats in Tehran on Sunday that Tehran hoped Washington would choose diplomacy but warned that Iran was prepared to respond if the US again chose military action.
On Thursday, sources told Reuters that Iran was preparing a broader and more forceful response if Washington resumed large-scale military attacks.
“If they again move towards military solutions, we are more prepared than before and will take whatever action is necessary to defend ourselves,” Araghchi said on Sunday.
Army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia told Fars news agency on Sunday Iran would upgrade the range of its missiles.

articles.title: Reaching the core: could Russia cut Ukrainians off from the internet and mobile communications?
articles.body:
Reaching the core: could Russia cut Ukrainians off from the internet and mobile communications?
Over the past week, the Kremlin has been expanding its campaign of terror to include new targets. In addition to hitting energy infrastructure and logistics hubs, Russia is now attacking the data centres that house equipment used by internet service providers, government services, banks and other digital systems, launching a wave of strikes on buildings where vital telecoms infrastructure is concentrated.
Telecoms industry representatives say it is not possible to cut Kyiv or Ukraine off from the internet by hitting data centres. There is no single facility whose destruction would take the country offline. But the objective of these attacks is not merely to carry out acts of terror. The goal is not the total destruction of the internet, but to degrade internet quality and overload backup routes, which could increase latency and destabilise networks.
And that may not be the worst-case scenario. The Russians have also started targeting mobile operator infrastructure, which may have more far-reaching consequences. Could these attacks disrupt communications across Ukraine? Where are the weak points in the country's telecoms infrastructure, and why is it that mobile networks could turn out to be significantly more vulnerable? Read on to find out.
From data centres to mobile network operators
On 23 September, Russian drones attacked a building in central Kyiv that housed one of the capital's data centres. A business centre was hit by several jet-powered Shahed drones in the course of an hour, and a fire then broke out.
Later that day, drones struck a similar data centre in another part of the city, and that evening, Russian forces hit yet another facility housing a data centre.
In one day, Russia had attacked at least three data centres in different parts of Kyiv. All housed equipment belonging to internet service providers. Some, notably the cloud service Fex.net, reported disruptions to their services. Ukraine's Ministry of Digital Transformation said around 100,000 users had problems accessing the internet.
Ekonomichna Pravda estimates that at least nine data centres in Kyiv may have been targeted since September, some of them more than once. The Protasiv Yar business centre, which housed the Cosmonova data centre, has been hit twice. Cosmonova suspended operations at the site as a result.
Four days later, the Russians turned their attention to mobile operators' infrastructure. Kyivstar, Ukraine's largest mobile operator, reported that a drone had struck one of its buildings, and Russia's Defence Ministry claimed that equipment belonging to Vodafone Ukraine had been damaged.
Internet service providers and mobile operators have suffered attacks to their networks before, but since 23 September the attacks have been on a different scale. Several data centres were hit within a few days, including some facilities that are critical to the telecoms industry.
For instance, a Russian attack destroyed a data centre that housed infrastructure belonging to hosting provider MiroHost. Founder Oleksandr Olshanskyi said MiroHost won't be able to bring its Ukraine-based infrastructure back online for at least the next three months.
Government digital services have also been disrupted, including state registries and electronic registration at centres run by Ukraine's Ministry of Internal Affairs that provide administrative services related to vehicles and driving licences.
The attacks on data centres have affected television broadcasts too. Disruptions have been reported by Army TV, Novyny.Live, We Are Ukraine, Pershyi, STB, 1+1, Channel 5, Suspilne Sport and Suspilne Culture.
Further evidence of the attacks is contained in a video posted by the Varyag Brigade, which is regarded as one of Russia's elite drone units alongside the better-known Rubicon unit. In the footage, Russian military personnel claim to have struck at least 11 data centres in Kyiv.
The exact dates of the strikes shown in the video cannot be established, but some appear to have taken place between 23 and 27 September. The footage clearly shows a strike on the Datagroup data centre on 25 September.
Read more: Fahrenheit 451: Russia has destroyed one-third of the books printed in Ukraine this year
The Ukrainian authorities had to respond. Following a meeting of the Staff of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said specific decisions had been taken to protect data centres and other critical communications infrastructure. The government is preparing for the worst. Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said the risk of widespread internet disruptions will persist for as long as Russia continues its strikes.
There is no one-size-fits-all way to protect this infrastructure. Some equipment can be moved underground; some can migrate to cloud environments or be relocated abroad. For some systems, a combination of these approaches may be used.
The government has allocated UAH 518.3 million (about US$11.5 million) to establish backup environments at separate locations, cloud infrastructure, and additional sites for state information systems. The funds will also be used to purchase server equipment, software, and data backup and recovery systems.
What happens if a data centre is attacked?
Much of the digital infrastructure Ukrainians rely on every day is built around data centres. The servers and storage systems they house keep websites, apps, state registers and banking services running.
Data centres are critical for internet service providers, as they house essential resources such as web, email and Domain Name System (DNS) servers, cloud infrastructure, and equipment belonging to providers and their clients.
Dmytro Kokhmaniuk, an expert on internet infrastructure and DNS, says some companies rent capacity in several data centres, others have their own facilities, and some combine both approaches. Spreading infrastructure across multiple sites helps make networks more resilient.
Repairing a data centre after an attack is a complex and lengthy process. "It's not just a room full of servers," Kokhmaniuk says. "It's a vast engineering system that includes a power supply, generators, cooling systems, ventilation, physical access control and network infrastructure. Damage to one or more of these elements can render the entire facility inoperable."
Consequently, a strike on a data centre can disrupt its operations even if the servers themselves escape damage. That does not necessarily mean, however, that the data stored there would be lost.
If up-to-date backups are stored at another independent site, the data can be restored. But getting everything back up and running requires computing resources, system configuration, and time. The impact of an attack therefore depends on how the particular service is set up and operated.
Since the start of Russia's full-scale war, a significant proportion of Ukraine's state registers and digital infrastructure has been moved to cloud services and backup environments in other countries.
So even if Russia destroys a Ukrainian data centre, the resulting outage may not last long. The attack may, however, cause temporary disruptions, loss of access and damage to equipment, and make it necessary to repair or relocate infrastructure.
Internet connectivity must also be restored separately. Damage to routers or an internet provider's cables can cut users off even when the service itself continues to operate. In that case, access can be restored using backup routes and equipment that survived intact, or by repairing the damaged network.
Internet speeds may drop
The events of 23 September offer some insight into what Russia may be trying to achieve by targeting Ukrainian network infrastructure.
One of the organisations affected that day was the internet service provider Pavutyna, which notified users of disruptions to its network. Co-owner and director Oleksandr Arutiunian said it was the third strike on the company's infrastructure, but the latest attack hit equipment at several locations almost simultaneously.
"The first two attacks were less disruptive because the backup systems worked better and the damage didn't all happen at the same time," Arutiunian says. "During the third attack, two locations were hit at once. The network could not recover automatically, so some users were left without a connection for between one and two hours. Repair crews then brought the network back online."
It appears that the Russians' target is not so much individual government services as the infrastructure that provides internet access. To this end, they are striking large data centres that house equipment used by several providers.
The telecoms industry representatives interviewed by Ekonomichna Pravda say these attacks cannot cut Ukrainians off from the internet entirely, because providers' network nodes are not only located in data centres.
"Networks have become much more decentralised in recent years," Arutiunian explains. "An operator can have far more than just one, two or five nodes. If necessary, backup equipment can be deployed at another site. In many cases this happens automatically, and engineers only need to step in when the damage is more serious."
If Ukrainian networks have numerous connections and backup routes, then what can Russia realistically achieve by attacking data centres?
Ekonomichna Pravda's sources say providers' network nodes and internet exchange points (IXPs) could potentially be targets. Network nodes support the operation of providers' networks, while IXPs allow different networks to exchange data. There are around 20 IXPs in Ukraine, and their equipment can be located at a single site or several.
The destruction of some of these facilities would not result in a nationwide internet blackout. As long as alternative connections are intact, internet service providers could reroute traffic through other operators, direct connections and international IXPs, just as traffic is diverted when a road is closed. Networks without an alternative route, however, could lose connectivity if their infrastructure is damaged.
The problem may lie elsewhere. Backup routes often have less capacity and are not set up to handle additional traffic. This could result in slower internet speeds and dropped connections for users.
That is what happened to internet provider Fiberlink after Russian attacks damaged the infrastructure of one of its backbone partners. The company rerouted traffic through a backup channel and warned users that internet speeds could temporarily drop. Further damage could lead to more significant disruptions.
According to Kokhmaniuk, poorer connection quality and slower data transfer speeds could be likely. In any event, operators will also have to absorb the additional cost of repairing infrastructure, deploying emergency repair crews and constructing backup lines. If the attacks continue, this could ultimately drive up the cost of broadband for subscribers.
"Operators will need to decentralise their networks further and expand the number of nodes and backup sites, which will increase the cost of providing services," Arutiunian says. "They will need more equipment, more staff and more resources to maintain and support this infrastructure."
Mobile network operator infrastructure
Mobile communications are another area of concern. If Russia continues to hit facilities belonging to mobile network operators, as it did on 27 September, this could have more serious consequences than attacks on data centres.
The Russians would not need to strike tens of thousands of base stations. The mobile core network, which manages subscriber registration, calls, text messages and mobile internet access, may be a far more vulnerable target.
If attacks were to disrupt critical functions of a core network beyond what its backup systems can handle, the consequences could be similar to those of the cyberattack on Kyivstar, which left millions of subscribers without access to calls, text messages or mobile internet.
Operators maintain backup infrastructure, but a fully-fledged mobile core network cannot simply be replicated by installing spare equipment at another node. Ekonomichna Pravda's sources estimate that building an additional core could cost each operator US$40-50 million. How many layers of redundancy would be needed if attacks on this infrastructure became sustained is an open question.
Ekonomichna Pravda's sources say the state and operators are taking steps to build more redundancy into critical network components. Some of these measures have been introduced only recently and will take time to implement. Russian attacks on mobile infrastructure could therefore pose a greater risk to communications.
What does this mean for users? In a critical situation, it's best to have more than one way of accessing the internet – for example, broadband from one provider and mobile internet from another. The more independent connections there are, the lower the risk of losing access during a large-scale attack.
Translated by Artem Yakymyshyn
Edited by Teresa Pearce

articles.title: US bombers pulled from RAF Fairford base after suspected terror plot
articles.body:
The US Air Force has pulled its bombers from RAF Fairford following an investigation into an alleged planned terror attack at the base.
The bombers were redeployed back to their home bases in the US, according to a Pentagon official who was not authorised to discuss sensitive military movements and spoke on Sunday on condition of anonymity.
A Pentagon spokesperson said: “While operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real time, we can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have redeployed to their home stations in the United States.”
At least 10 B-1 bombers of 12 flew out of Fairford on Sunday, including some that arrived on rotation less than a week ago, underlining the haste of the departure and the apparent significance given by the US to the threat.
There was no immediate comment from the UK Ministry of Defence, though the rapid pace of the withdrawal will heighten concerns in the area around the RAF base in Gloucestershire.
According to reporting by US media, the withdrawal appears to be in response to fresh or renewed security concerns about safety on the base.
A report in the New York Times said: “American officials on Sunday declined to specify the nature of the new information that prompted the rapid withdrawal of the Air Force bombers, some of which had just arrived in the past week as part of a normal rotation of forces.
“One US official said the new information was part of the same threat warnings that surfaced three weeks ago, but specific details and a sense of urgency spiked in the past 24 hours, alarming commanders.”
A dual British-Iranian national was arrested in central London last week on suspicion of plotting a terror attack, following a security incident at RAF Fairford in late September. In total, six people have been taken into custody and then released on bail during the investigation.
British authorities have linked the incident to Tehran. Iran has denied involvement.
RAF Fairford, located 100 miles (160km) west of London, has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East.
Its use in recent months came after then prime minister Keir Starmer granted Washington permission to use British bases for “defensive” strikes against Tehran.
The US military still maintains a sizeable presence in the Middle East. On Thursday, a US official said the recently deployed USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier as well as the USS Makin Island amphibious readiness group – a group of ships that together carry more than 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines – were heading for the region. The official said the move could result in three carriers being in the region as early as the end of October.

Mathernová noted that Russia is trying to make the EU reduce its support for Ukraine, but that this only makes the EU more determined to continue that support. articles.title: Tory conference 2026: What POLITICO reporters are watching for
articles.body:
BIRMINGHAM, England — Britain’s largest opposition party wants to show it’s still on the electoral pitch during an annual gathering that kicks off Sunday.
Despite Conservative Leader Kemi Badenoch consolidating her position and seeing improved personal ratings, the party is still far from its government heyday, and faces an ongoing challenge on the right from Nigel Farage’s populist Reform UK.
Here’s what POLITICO’s team of reporters will be watching for as the Conservatives gather in Birmingham.
Advertisement
U.K. Political Editor Dan Bloom
My biggest question for Badenoch’s speech at 11 a.m. Wednesday will be: can she end Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s honeymoon?
Since July, Labour has jumped to 26% in the polls while the Tories lag behind Reform on 19%. There will simply be fewer lobbyists and hangers-on than at Labour’s jamboree.
Badenoch will spend this week arguing that Burnham, with his crusade against “40 years of neoliberalism,” has ushered in the kind of classic left-right ideological fight that she relishes. Expect her to bang on about cutting welfare to fund defense — two weak points for Labour. And the self-described “badass Kemi” plans to be more abrasive than Burnham, who went out of his way not to attack anyone in his speech.
I reckon two things will decide if she can cut through: her personal brand, and how far she can differentiate the Tories from Labour and Reform (plus, well, her own party from 2024). She will try to paint the Tories as the party of fiscal responsibility but that’s a crowded marketplace. It’s worked for the Conservatives in the past but we aren’t in two-party politics anymore — though admittedly, the five-party split has become less dramatic since the summer.
There will be economic policy announcements but perhaps not on the scale of last year’s pledge to scrap stamp duty. Badenoch has talked about getting rid of inheritance tax but aides appear to be suggesting an announcement isn’t ready.
I can’t wait to see the peacocking by would-be candidates for a general election. Tory aides are shouting from the hills that they are on a “war footing” and candidate selection is ramping up. Some of the high-profile Tories who were rejected for being too centrist are swerving this year’s conference, but former West Midlands Mayor Andy Street will be prominent on the fringe. Critics complain that Badenoch has bulldozed the transepts off her party’s ideological church.
Advertisement
And, of course, I’d ask questions about a coalition. There is no love lost between the Tories and Reform but all recent polls suggest they would have to team up to have any chance of running a government. Will she pull any punches against Farage … or Restore Britain chief Rupert Lowe, whose vote-splitting might help her in the end?
Senior Foreign and Defense Correspondent Esther Webber
I’ll be really interested to see how the party is positioning itself against what we know so far about Ed Miliband’s agenda as foreign secretary — so whether there’s any dissent over new sanctions introduced by Labour on Israeli E1 settlements.
Miliband has just begun to signal a potentially more conciliatory approach to China as an alternative locus of power and investment versus the U.S., so I’ll be looking at whether the Conservatives think this is a weak point where they can redouble attacks on Labour.
There’s also the question of artificial intelligence regulation and which camp the Tories are situating themselves in. Will they agree with the government on the need for a globally coordinated effort, or back U.S. President Donald Trump’s zero-regulation stance?
Finally, here’s a side plot: Are there any signs that former Home Secretary Priti Patel, traditionally a conference fan favorite, is actually doing anything in her new role in coordinating cooperation between the Tories and other parties internationally?
London Influence Reporter John Johnston
With little detail so far about Burnham’s plans for business, and many corporate execs pondering if Farage’s Reform has hit its peak, this Tory conference will be a vital opportunity for the party to try and show it is building back towards being a credible alternative.
Advertisement
Since the 2024 general election, many businesses and lobbying firms have sent only a skeleton staff to Tory conference. But I’ve heard that extra corporate passes and tickets to the standalone Business Day have been snapped up in the last few months. So, attendance may be healthier — even if most still won’t be splashing out on panel events or exhibition stands.
Business leaders remain skeptical about the prospect of an early general election. But as the official opposition, the Conservatives have the potential to help industry shine a spotlight on concerns and push issues up the political agenda if one comes. At last year’s conference, many public affairs pros felt the Tories lacked the ideas, unity and leadership to do that. My focus this year will be figuring out if that assessment has shifted.
Energy Reporter Abby Wallace
The Conservatives have come a long way from the party that, in government, enshrined net-zero targets in law. Badenoch has been clear about the direction she wants to take the party in: ditching legally-binding climate targets and drilling for more oil and gas in the North Sea.
The party’s leader has even suggested that former colleagues who still support the target will not be welcome back on the Tory benches. I’ll be looking out for whether that U-turn at the top has fully filtered through the party.
While energy bills have surged on the back of war in Iran, the party has been pressing Labour ministers to prioritize cutting costs in the system. For the Conservatives, that means ditching some support for renewables and a bigger role for gas and nuclear in the future. I’ll be keeping an ear on whether there is any pressure from the opposition for ministers to intervene ahead of what will be a difficult winter of price rises too.
The future of the North Sea, including looming decisions on Rosebank and Jackdaw, will no doubt spring up on the fringes — especially after the Conservatives clinched the Aberdeen South by-election following a campaign focused on oil and gas drilling.
Advertisement
Financial Services Reporter Eleanor Myers
Andrew Griffith will be stepping up this party conference, having been promoted to shadow chancellor earlier this year to replace his more mild-mannered colleague Mel Stride.
Griffith was a bigwig in business before he entered parliament, and as a former City minister, I’ll be watching whether he focuses his ire on the prospect of Labour raising bank taxes in the budget, which is now less than a month away.
Griffith will make his big speech on how to get Britain growing again at 2 p.m. Monday. Growth was the favored buzzword of former Chancellor Rachel Reeves, and has been heartily adopted by her successor John Healey, although how to achieve it remains a challenge amid soaring debt and rising interest rates. I’m interested to see whether the Conservatives propose a solution.
Senior Technology Reporter Frank Hersey
This conference is a chance for Badenoch’s team to establish any sort of differentiation between Tory tech policy and that of the other parties. This has been getting harder as parties’ approaches have coalesced. Labour committed to a pro-growth agenda for AI under former Prime Minister Keir Starmer with planned regulatory reforms to match. Tory plans for a social media ban for under-16s were eventually (and reluctantly) grasped by Labour. The Tories were further hemmed in by Reform banking the low-tax, low-regulation space.
I’ll be looking to see if the party can get ahead in any policy areas or if it has to pick new ones to do so. Among all the parties, there’s perhaps most interest in what the Conservatives say on tech — as their policy ideas in this space are feeling overdue.
Senior Trade Reporter Sophie Inge
The fightback against Burnham’s pledge to explore closer ties with the EU is expected to continue in Birmingham, after Badenoch warned that Britain shouldn’t be “having arguments which started 10 years ago.”
Deputy Leader Alex Burghart has already pledged to “reverse” the Brexit reset, warning that plans for an agrifood deal with the bloc risk undermining the U.K.’s trading relationship with the U.S., among other countries.

articles.title: German Chancellor Merz arrives in Kyiv amid Russian attacks
articles.body:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Kyiv on Sunday as air raid sirens and explosions sounded across the Ukrainian capital, where another Russian drone strike hit the Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River.
Merz travelled to Ukraine for talks with President Volodymyr Zelensky as Germany prepared further military and energy support and deeper cooperation with Ukraine's defence industry.
Four air raid alerts sounded in Kyiv on Sunday morning, Reuters reported. Air defence systems were also heard operating across the city.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said a strike damaged the roadway of the Northern Bridge and a heating main, disrupting hot water supplies in the Desnyanskyi district. No casualties from the bridge strike had been reported.
The attack marked the second consecutive day that the Northern Bridge had been hit. The Southern Bridge was targeted several times earlier in the week. Major bridges in Kyiv have faced Russian strikes for four consecutive days.
Merz and Zelensky paid tribute to Ukrainian soldiers at a memorial in Independence Square and visited a National Academy of Sciences building damaged in an earlier Russian strike.
"Ukraine is facing decisive weeks. That is why I travelled to Kyiv today with the message: You can rely on us," Merz wrote on X.
German government officials told Reuters that Merz would announce the release of €1 billion in military assistance and €350 million for repairs to Ukraine's energy infrastructure.
Germany and Ukraine are also expected to finalise an agreement on joint drone production. Reuters reported that cooperation is expected to include interceptor drones designed to counter high-speed Russian attack drones. Plans also cover the development and production of weapons with ranges exceeding 1,000km.
Merz travelled with Economy Minister Katherina Reiche and representatives from German companies including Siemens Energy, Hensoldt, Diehl Defence and Quantum Systems.
The chancellor is also expected to raise reforms sought by Ukraine's European partners, including measures against corruption.
Russia's Foreign Ministry said on Saturday that Moscow would continue what it described as retaliatory strikes following Ukrainian attacks inside Russia. It also urged foreign nationals and diplomatic personnel to avoid travelling to Ukraine.
Zelensky said Russia launched 135 attack drones across Ukraine overnight, including more than 50 jet-powered models. He said one person was killed in an attack on a pharmaceutical warehouse in Sumy and six people were injured after a communications facility was struck in Dnipro.
"If Russia is not stopped, sooner or later its war machine will turn against us," Merz said.

Ukrainian forces destroyed a Russian Pantsir-S2 air defense system using FP-2 strike drones, with footage showing the system burning before its ammunition detonated and tore the vehicle apart.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukrainian open-source monitoring channel Exilenova+ on October 3, the Pantsir-S2 had been interfering with Ukrainian drone operations and preventing UAVs from reaching targets deeper behind Russian lines.

The Pantsir-S2 is an upgraded version of Russia’s Pantsir family of short-range air defense systems. It combines surface-to-air missiles with 30 mm automatic cannons and is designed to engage aircraft, missiles, and unmanned aerial vehicles.
The S2 variant features an upgraded target-detection radar intended to improve the system’s ability to detect and track aerial targets.

articles.title: U.S. Air Force adds $12M for AI agents on doomsday plane
articles.body:
- The U.S. Air Force added $12.1 million to Scale AI's contract for agentic AI on the E-4C Survivable Airborne Operations Center, raising it to $44.3 million.
- The work runs through Nov. 5, 2027, with $5 million in fiscal 2026 research funds obligated at award.
The U.S. Air Force has added $12.1 million to a contract with Scale AI to develop artificial intelligence agents for the E-4C Survivable Airborne Operations Center, the new “doomsday plane” meant to keep U.S. leaders in command of the military, including nuclear forces, if ground command centers are destroyed.
The modification raises the total value of the San Francisco company’s contract from $32.2 million to $44.3 million, the U.S. Department of War said. The work will be done in San Francisco and is expected to run through Nov. 5, 2027. The U.S. Air Force obligated $5 million in fiscal 2026 research and development funds at award.
The notice does not say what tasks the AI agents will perform aboard the aircraft, whether they will run on the plane itself or on ground systems that support it, or how much human control will be built in.
Agentic AI goes a step beyond chatbots that answer questions. These systems can plan and carry out multi-step tasks on their own, such as gathering and sorting information, drafting options or managing workflows, with people supervising or approving key decisions. On a command aircraft packed with communications gear and a battle staff, that could mean helping crews handle large volumes of messages and data during a crisis, though the U.S. Air Force has not described its plans.
The original contract was awarded earlier this year through the Air Force Research Laboratory’s Information Directorate in Rome, New York. The latest modification was issued by the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center at Hanscom Air Force Base, Massachusetts.
The E-4C will replace the E-4B Nightwatch, a fleet of four heavily modified Boeing 747-200s that first flew in the 1970s and serve as the National Airborne Operations Center. The aircraft are hardened against the effects of nuclear blasts and can be refueled in flight, allowing them to stay aloft for long periods while the president, defense secretary and senior commanders direct forces from the air.
Sierra Nevada Corp. won a $13 billion contract in April 2024 to build the replacement. The company bought used Boeing 747-8I airliners from Korean Air and is converting them in Dayton, Ohio, adding protection against radiation and electromagnetic pulse, new communications antennas, computers and mission systems. The first E-4C test aircraft flew on Aug. 7, 2025, and flight and ground testing is continuing through 2026 before mission equipment is installed. Deliveries are scheduled to finish by July 2036.
Scale AI, best known for labeling data used to train AI models, has become a major supplier of AI tools to the U.S. military. In March 2025, it won the Defense Innovation Unit’s Thunderforge project to bring AI agents into military planning and operations, working with Anduril and Microsoft. Earlier this year, the Pentagon’s Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office raised the ceiling on another Scale AI agreement from $100 million to $500 million. Meta holds a minority stake in the company.

articles.title: Diplomatic path to ending war remains open: Iran FM Araghchi
articles.body:
Iran’s top diplomat made the remarks during a meeting with ambassadors and heads of diplomatic missions in Iran on Sunday, stressing that the diplomatic path to ending war remains open.
Araghchi first pointed to Iran’s delegation attended at 81st UN General Assembly in New York last month, stating that Iranian delegation had a strong, influential and effective presence in New York this year.
Iran’s response to any military action will be stronger than before, the Iranian foreign minister reiterated.
Iran showed at the UN General Assembly that it has solutions for both war and peace, while efforts to isolate it have failed, he said, adding, “New US sanctions will achieve nothing. The US has failed both militarily and diplomatically.”
It has become clear to everyone that Iran remains as serious about diplomacy and finding a peaceful solution as it is about defending itself, he underlined.
“We remain firm and resolute in defending ourselves and advancing diplomacy. Should our enemies opt for a military confrontation, they will face a response far more forceful than in the past, whereas if they seek diplomatic avenues, we are prepared to reach an honorable solution through diplomatic channels.”
Araghchi then pointed to the expulsion of Iranian diplomats by the US in New York, emphasizing, “The claim made by the Americans that they expelled Iranian diplomats is truly bizarre. It demonstrated just how angry they were about the presence of the Iranian delegation.”
Referring to the meetings held with the Persian Gulf Arab states’ officials, Araghchi stated, "All of these meetings were held in a friendly atmosphere, and we have embarked on a new path for relations with these countries. Our brothers in the Persian Gulf are aligned with us, and a shared determination to establish stability—with the participation of the countries themselves—is being pursued."
Referring to the meetings held with European countries, he stated, "We hope the Europeans will reconsider their approach toward Iran. The NATO Secretary General’s admission regarding participation in a war against Iran was a grave matter. He [NATO chief] stated that over 5,000 fighter jets took off from bases in Europe, and we await an explanation from European countries. Our proposal to these nations is to engage in dialogue with Iran and avoid being drawn into any warmongering by the US and the Zionist regime."

articles.title: Iran vows stronger response to military attack
articles.body:
Iran vows stronger response to military attack
Araghchi says Iran remains ready for a diplomatic solution to US conflict
TEHRAN — Iran is ready for a diplomatic solution to its conflict with the US, but if Washington again chooses a military course, Tehran is more prepared than before to defend itself and will deliver a stronger response, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday.
Addressing ambassadors and representatives of foreign countries based in Tehran at the Foreign Ministry, Araghchi said Iran remained firm and serious on both fronts — defending itself and pursuing diplomacy.
“If our enemies again choose the path of military confrontation, they will receive a stronger response than before, and we will defend ourselves more powerfully than before,” he said. “And if they are seeking diplomatic avenues, we remain ready to reach a just and dignified solution to end this war through diplomacy.”
Araghchi said Iran hoped the US would choose “the path of wisdom and rationality,” stressing that there was no military or sanctions-based solution to the conflict.
“The only solution that can work is a negotiated solution based on justice and fairness, and a dignified and diplomatic solution,” he said, adding that such an approach could provide a final way out of what he described as the “illegal and unjust aggression” launched against Iran.
Diplomatic outreach remains strong
Araghchi also highlighted Iran’s diplomatic activity during the recent UN General Assembly meetings in New York, saying the Iranian delegation had played a strong and effective role.
“I met with 42 foreign ministers, and the president met with 10 heads of state in New York,” he said.
He said Iran had clearly explained its positions in New York and that the level of interest shown by different countries in meeting with Iranian officials, learning about Tehran’s views and hearing its proposals had been “very significant.”
Araghchi said this had demonstrated the failure of what he described as an attempt by some in the US to isolate Iran.
“The perception that some people in the US may have had that they could turn Iran into an isolated country had completely failed,” he said, adding that Iran had acted in New York as “a powerful country respected by the international community” and demonstrated that it continued to have “rational positions” and solutions for both war and peace.
Iranian diplomats, he said, had been highly active at the General Assembly and had conveyed the voice of the Iranian people to the international community.
“We were present in all fields and conveyed the voice of the Iranian people to the world,” Araghchi said, adding that Iran had delivered its people's message in favor of peace and rational solutions.
He also said Tehran had clearly explained its conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, stressing that all of those conditions were consistent with commitments that the US must accept.
Tehran dismisses US claim over Iranian delegation
Araghchi also rejected a claim from the US that the Iranian delegation had been expelled from the country.
“Regardless of whether this claim is true or not, since we went and returned according to our own pre-planned schedule, the claim made by the Americans is truly strange,” he said.
He argued that the claim was contradictory because, on the one hand, it amounted to an admission that the US had violated its obligations as the host country of the United Nations, while on the other hand it demonstrated how angry Washington had become over the presence of the
Iranian delegation in the US.
‘No solution through more sanctions’
Araghchi said the US had already failed both militarily and diplomatically and would gain nothing from imposing additional sanctions.
“The US has lost both in war and in diplomacy in the past,” he said. “Trying new sanctions will also be of no benefit to them. There is no military solution and no solution based on more sanctions.”
He reiterated that Tehran remained prepared for both military defense and diplomacy.
“We remain firm and serious in both areas of defending ourselves and advancing diplomacy,” he said.
Calls on Europe to reconsider its position
Araghchi said he had also held extensive discussions with European countries and described those talks as “very frank.”
“We hope that European countries will reconsider their approach toward the Islamic Republic of Iran,” he said.
He referred to what he described as a significant admission by the NATO secretary-general regarding European involvement in the US war against Iran.
“The admission by the NATO secretary-general that European countries participated in the US war against Iran was a serious admission,” Araghchi said.
According to Araghchi, the NATO chief had explicitly said that more than 5,000 US fighter jets had taken off from bases in Europe to attack Iran.
“We are still waiting for European countries to answer this question: Why did they play an effective role in this war against Iran?” he said.
Despite his criticism, Araghchi said Iran's proposal to European countries was to establish dialogue with Tehran and avoid any participation in renewed efforts by the US and Israel to escalate the conflict.
“Our proposal to these countries is to establish dialogue with the Islamic Republic of Iran and avoid any participation in renewed warmongering by the US and the Zionist regime,” he said.
Seven-day plan could reopen Hormuz
Araghchi said Iran's most important diplomatic initiative was a proposal it had presented for resolving the disputes between Iran and the US and ending the ongoing war.
He referred to the initiative as the seven-day plan, saying that acceptance of the proposal would allow the Strait of Hormuz to be reopened within seven days.
“The most important of all these issues is the plan that the Islamic Republic of Iran has presented for resolving the existing disputes and the ongoing war between Iran and the US,” he said.
“This plan is known as the seven-day plan, and if it is accepted, the Strait of Hormuz will be reopened within seven days.”
Araghchi's remarks came as Tehran reiterated that it remained open to diplomacy while warning that any renewed military action would be met with a stronger response.

articles.title: Moscow vows to ramp up strikes on Ukraine after Zelensky’s threat
articles.body:
Moscow vows to ramp up strikes on Ukraine after Zelensky’s threat
Russia will intensify strikes on military and defense-related facilities in Ukraine in response to Vladimir Zelensky’s threat to increase attacks on Russian oil refineries, the Defense Ministry warned.
In a statement on Sunday, the ministry said it has “taken note” of the Ukrainian leader’s promise a day earlier to step up attacks on Russian oil refineries in response to strikes on bridges across the Dnieper River in Kiev.
Russia has already ramped up strikes on military-related logistics – including the key port of Odessa – and the defense industrial base in recent weeks in response to Zelensky’s botched 40-day PR ‘pressure campaign’, which included long-range strikes targeting oil refineries and civilian infrastructure deep inside Russia.
“Following Zelensky’s statement today, strikes by the Russian Armed Forces on military and military-industrial facilities, as well as related infrastructure in Kiev and other regions of Ukraine, will be intensified,” the ministry said in a statement on Sunday.
People in Ukraine should blame only the head of the Kiev regime for this. It is Zelensky who bears full personal and political responsibility for it.
The Defense Ministry reiterated that the Russian military has been responding to Kiev’s attacks on civilian targets in Russia that were meant to disrupt the State Duma election. It cited strikes on polling stations that killed six civilians, an attempted mass attack involving more than 1,600 Ukrainian strike drones against civilian sites in Moscow on September 19-20, and drone attacks aimed at disrupting the St. Petersburg International Economic Forum in June.
It also cited a strike on residential areas in Belgorod that killed and wounded civilians and damaged apartment buildings, houses, and vehicles.
President Vladimir Putin acknowledged that the strikes on oil refineries have cost around 1% of Russia’s GDP, but noted that the damaged facilities are being quickly restored, and that the nation’s energy system is operating with significant reserve capacity. Following Russia’s retaliatory strikes, Ukraine no longer has a steelmaking industry, he added.

articles.title: ‘Everyone knows’ Kiev is embezzling Western aid – ex-Polish PM
articles.body:
‘Everyone knows’ Kiev is embezzling Western aid – ex-Polish PM
Ukrainian officials are embezzling foreign financial aid, former Polish Prime Minister Leszek Miller has said, adding that Kiev’s backers are well aware of the corruption but prefer not to ask questions.
Speaking on the ‘Jankowski Kontra’ podcast on Polsat News on Saturday, Miller called for suspending aid to Ukraine until Kiev accounts for previously supplied weapons and funds.
“Nobody’s asking what happened to the 300 tanks we sent in the first phase. What happened to the heavy equipment, the lighter equipment... Nobody’s asking what happened to the billions of euros we donated. Mr. Zelensky simply comes and says, ‘Give it’, and we give it,” Miller stated.
Asked whether he suspected that funds transferred to Ukraine were being embezzled, Miller replied: “Of course, everyone knows it.”The veteran politician argued that Warsaw should demand an accounting of how its assistance has been used and halt further support if Kiev fails to provide one.
“This is a fundamental issue: I’ll lend you the money, but give me a report on what you did with the previous installment,” Miller stated. “Without that help, there is no Ukraine… But we are not a country that is overflowing with wealth… We have obligations to our own citizens, and we cannot simply throw away money and equipment indiscriminately.”
Poland has been one of Kiev’s staunchest backers in its conflict with Russia, pouring billions into military, financial and humanitarian aid while serving as a crucial hub for Western supplies. Yet relations have increasingly soured over Kiev’s honoring of Ukrainian Nazi collaborators linked to the World War II-era Volhynia massacres, in which UPA militants, linked to the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN), killed at least 100,000 ethnic Poles.
Warsaw recognizes the killings as genocide, while Kiev honors figures including OUN leader Stepan Bandera. Tensions flared again this year after Zelensky bestowed the title ‘Heroes of the UPA’ on the Ukrainian Special Operations Center North military unit. In the aftermath, Polish President Karol Nawrocki stripped him of the country’s highest honor, politicians on both sides renounced state decorations, and Warsaw threatened to obstruct Ukraine’s EU accession.
Relations have also been strained by mounting opposition to Ukrainian refugees. A July CBOS survey found that 52% of Poles now opposed accepting them, against 42% in favor – a sharp reversal from the overwhelming support seen after Kiev’s conflict with Moscow escalated in 2022. Tensions deepened earlier this month after a 31-year-old Ukrainian man stabbed five people at a Benedictine abbey in Jaroslaw, killing a priest.
Poland is also not alone in questioning funding for Kiev. Despite receiving billions in Western assistance over the past four years, Ukraine faces a severe cash squeeze and has been pressing European backers for more money. But a string of high-level graft scandals has heightened scrutiny in Brussels, the largest of which centers on an alleged $100 million kickback scheme at state nuclear operator Energoatom, which was reportedly led by Timur Mindich, a former business partner of Vladimir Zelensky.
Western-backed investigators have uncovered multiple other graft schemes involving Ukrainian officials, including one reported earlier this month in which they allegedly embezzled more than $3 million through the delivery of used Soviet-made metro cars donated by Poland.
Against that backdrop, the EU this week rebuffed Kiev’s bid to fast-track its latest €90 billion support loan, making clear that further funds depend on Ukraine delivering promised anti-corruption and governance reforms.

articles.title: External affairs minister S Jaishankar says US has chosen to become 'lonelier power'
articles.body:
External affairs minister S Jaishankar addresses the 62nd Munich Security Conference in New Delhi
NEW DELHI: Foreign minister S Jaishankar said US had deliberately chosen to become a "lonelier power", while reiterating Russia's longstanding support for India."At a time when much of the world preferred backing a military regime next to us (Pakistan), Russia was a country with which our relations were very good, and we are shaped in many ways by that legacy," he said at Munich Leaders Meeting here.He said India's Russia-Ukraine conflict approach had moved beyond just the advocacy of dialogue, suggesting India might now be looking to actively mediate.
World today is marked by America’s radical repositioning and China’s rise, says Jaishankar
Both Moscow and Kyiv have said recently that India had come up with ideas and proposals to bring an end to the war. Unlike China and others that have looked to mediate, India had so far supported global peace efforts — advocating dialogue between the parties — but had not come up its own proposal, reflecting its emphasis on bilateral resolution of disputes.Offering a teaser on India’s proposal, Jaishankar said India is looking to address some immediate concerns that both Russia and Ukraine have on “grain exports, energy exports, non-attack possibilities”.“We would like to see an end to this conflict. This will require dialogue and diplomacy. We have been advocating it for many years, and in recent months we have got a little bit more involved beyond advocacy. We have conversations with both Russia and Ukraine in this regard.
We are trying to be helpful, starting with the Black Sea safety of shipping issue,” said the minister, speaking at the Munich Leaders Meeting here.Jaishankar had said during his visit to Ukraine last month — shortly after PM Narendra Modi’s message to Russian President Vladimir Putin to stop the “endless war” — that India was discussing ideas that could be developed for cessation of hostilities.
On Friday, while Putin announced Modi had very good ideas for peace, Ukraine’s foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said India had come up with the “broadest” peace proposal out of the four that it had received from other countries, including the US.This shift in India’s position seems driven by direct domestic fallout of the conflict, whether it’s commercial shipping disruptions in Black Sea or an intense blowback from US over India’s continued purchase of Russian crude.On US, Jaishankar said the world today was marked by a radical repositioning of the US, and also the rise of China.“The current system was significantly underwritten by the United States. That underwriting is diluting.” He underlined that the sharp competition between US and China was not limited to them alone. “It has led to weaponisation of any leverage that any country has. ”

articles.title: Trump says Iran dropped nuclear weapon plans
articles.body:

US President Donald Trump said on Oct. 3 Iran has virtually abandoned its drive to develop nuclear weapons because severe financial exhaustion and regional setbacks crippled Tehran's strategic leverage.
Speaking to reporters, Trump said Iranian authorities no longer possess the capability or ambition to produce an atomic bomb and are eager to negotiate a new settlement. "They have virtually given up any plans for nuclear weapons," he said.
Trump reiterated his position an Iranian nuclear weapon remains unacceptable, asserting earlier maximum pressure sanctions and subsequent economic isolation had drained Tehran's revenue before recent regional conflicts further weakened the government.
The remarks come as international observers continue to monitor Tehran's atomic program. The International Atomic Energy Agency reported earlier this year Iran had accumulated an enriched uranium stockpile with purity levels reaching 60 percent, just below the 90 percent threshold required for weapons-grade material.
Tehran has consistently maintained its atomic work remains exclusively civilian, focused on energy generation and medical research. The diplomatic dispute intensified in 2018 when the US unilaterally pulled out of the 2015 nuclear accord, formally known as the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, before reimposing sweeping banking and oil sanctions on the Islamic republic.

articles.title: USS George H.W. Bush anchors in Thailand for recreational visit after Middle East deployment
articles.body:
The US aircraft carrier George H.W. Bush arrived off Thailand's resort island of Phuket on Sunday with about 4,800 personnel aboard for a rest-and-recreation break after months of supporting US operations in the Middle East.
The Nimitz-class carrier had been operating in the Arabian Sea during the conflict with Iran, according to multiple media reports.
The carrier will anchor offshore, while crew members are expected to come ashore through Phuket Deep Sea Port and spend time on the popular southern resort island from October 4 to 9, local media reported.
A local mayor had estimated that each US service member from the Lincoln could spend up to 3,000 baht ($89) per day during the visit. Thailand is the United States' only treaty partner in mainland Southeast Asia.
The visit follows a five-day port call by the USS Abraham Lincoln at Laem Chabang in eastern Thailand last month, with about 5,000 sailors and Marines aboard.
US carrier Abraham Lincoln departs Thailand after respite visit
The nuclear-powered Lincoln was involved in the US naval blockade and combat operations in the war with Iran and, according to Democratic lawmakers, set a modern-day record for consecutive days at sea.
“We would like to thank the people of Thailand for their incredible hospitality,” US Navy Captain Dan Keeler, the Abraham Lincoln’s commanding officer, said in a statement after the carrier departed in early September.
Busloads of sailors and Marines wearing civilian clothes, many smiling and waving, started arriving at a hotel in the resort city of Pattaya, about 150 km (93 miles) southeast of Bangkok, shortly after their ships docked.

articles.title: Israel warned Germany of increased risk to US military bases, senior US official says - report
articles.body:
Israel warned Germany of an increased risk of attacks against US military bases on its territory, particularly Ramstein Air Base and Spangdahlem Air Base, The New York Times reported on Saturday, citing a senior US official.
Both Ramstein and Spangdahlem are used by NATO air forces, with the former serving as the headquarters for the United States Air Forces in Europe – Air Forces Africa and NATO Allied Air Command.
According to the report, the warning was issued following intelligence received in mid-September indicating the possibility of Iranian-backed attacks against US facilities in Europe, including RAF Fairford in the UK.
The intelligence assessments also included concerns about possible drone attacks, but did not point to a specific time or target.
On September 23, media outlets affiliated with Iran published remarks by a former senior Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps official who explicitly mentioned Ramstein Air Base as one of the facilities used by the US in its war against Iran.
Netanyahu says Israeli intelligence helped thwart UK attack
Also on Saturday, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu sharply criticized the British government in an interview with The Daily Mail, accusing it of "behaving like a rogue state" and appeasing what he called the "Islamist-leftist alliance."
Netanyahu said Israel had provided British security services with intelligence that helped thwart a deadly Iranian-backed attack on RAF Fairford.
"Had it not been for the intelligence we provided, the attack would probably have gone ahead, and we do not know how many Britons would have been killed," he claimed, adding: "They are appeasing their enemies and attacking those who defend them."
Netanyahu also claimed on Saturday that Israel had provided British security services with intelligence that helped thwart a deadly Iranian-backed attack on RAF Fairford.
Netanyahu addresses Flydubai incident and Iran
In the interview, Netanyahu also addressed an alleged attempt to crash a flydubai plane en route to Israel.
"As time passes, the picture is becoming clearer: The attacker underwent Islamist radicalization. He came to crash the plane with its passengers. We are investigating whether he was sent, and whoever sent him will pay a heavy price."
Speaking about the Iranian regime, Netanyahu said: "This regime will fall. Right now it is very weak, and [US] President [Donald] Trump's blockade is severely weakening the IRGC. Your day of freedom will come."
